speechtext:
First, Mr. Chairman, I should like to thank hon. members in all parts of the chamber for the contribution each has made in placing before the committee ideas and suggestions, all of which will receive full and complete consideration.
Possibly I should begin by answering the questions asked by the hon. member for Ottawa West. While I am not at liberty to refer particularly to the bill, may I say this. The national centennial administration tc which I made reference will have the righi to expend any moneys appropriated by parliament for the work of the administration or received by the administration through the conduct of its operations or by gift, donation, bequest or otherwise.
As to the second question asked by him, maj I say this. It is the purpose and object of this legislation when brought before the house to assure that the celebration to take place in 1967 shall be a national celebration representative, as I said earlier, of all the people of Canada, and naturally representative of all the political thinking of Canada. To that end provision will be made in the legislation so that each province will appoint

Canadian Centennial
two members to the organization to be set up in that connection known as the national conference on Canada's centennial.
I think that covers the two questions the hon. member brought before the committee, although earlier he made reference to an opportunity being given to the House of Commons each year during the next six years to express its views with regard to matters which, in the opinion of members, it might be necessary to discuss in order to improve and to expand the work of the conference or of the administration. While there is no definite plan in that connection I should think it would be considered the course of reason to give the house from time to time the opportunity to place its collective views before the government and, through the government, before the conference and the committee.
It has been a worth-while occasion as we forget for a moment those things that ordinarily separate us and as we deal with a matter of national importance, see the degree of unanimity that has been apparent here during the course of the discussion. There have been many plans. Someone has asked what the total expenditure will be. That, of course, is a matter of conjecture. It will depend upon the nature and extent of the celebration to take place. It will depend as well on the extent to which the provinces co-operate and make their contributions. I would also hope there would be many private organizations which would feel the urge to make a contribution to the objective we all have in mind, namely a declaration to all the world of Canada's attainment of its centennial and also of our plans for the future.
Indeed, I should not be surprised that the time is not too far removed when the Canada of today will have additional provinces. Confederation was greatly strengthened when Newfoundland became a member of it. That was a step which it had been hoped would be achieved in 1867 or shortly thereafter but which, by reason of circumstances, was postponed for some 80 years. There are other northern areas that are developing. As Canada spreads northward and as national development carries on still further in the direction of the pole-I refer to the developing population of those areas-we may yet see one province and possibly two added to the existing 10 within the lifetime of numbers of hon. members sitting in this chamber.
As I listened to the hon. member for St. Boniface I recalled the words of Sir George Etienne Cartier in 1867, at the time the nation had its beginning. His words were these:

The time has arrived to form a great nation, and X maintain that, as far as we are concerned, confederation has become necessary to our commerce, our prosperity, and our protection ...
The government is of the opinion that confederation is necessary, but it is ready to hear the honourable members on the other side who apparently intend to oppose it. I am aware that members of this House and a number of people in Upper Canada and the maritime provinces believe that a legislative union would be more advantageous than a confederation. As far as I am concerned, I believe that a single government could not deal properly with the private and local interests of the various sections or the various provinces. No other system is practicable but a federal system. It is pretended that it will be impossible to carry out confederation on account of differences of race and of religion. Those who hold that opinion are in error. It is precisely on account of the difference in races and local interests that the federal system should be established and that it will work well. We have often read in the newspapers-and there are public men who hold likewise-that it is a great evil to have such different races, such distinctions between French Canadians and English Canadians. I desire in this connection to vindicate the rights and merits of the French race in Canada. It will suffice to recall the efforts which the French Canadians made to uphold British power on this continent, and to show their attachment for the British crown in a time of trial...
Objection is made to our project, because of the words "a new nationality". But if we unite, we will form a political nationality independent of the national origin and religion of individuals. Some have regretted that we have a distinction of races, and have expressed the hope that, in time, this diversity will disappear. The idea of a fusion of all races is utopian; it is an impossibility. Distinctions of this character will always exist; diversity is the order of the physical, moral and political world. As to the objection that we cannot form a great nation because lower Canada is French and Catholic, upper Canada English and Protestant, and the maritime provinces mixed, it is futile. Take, for example, the United Kingdom, inhabited as it is by three great races. Has the diversity of races been an obstacle to the progress and welfare of Great Britain? Have not the three races united by their combined qualities, their energy and their courage, contributed to the glory of the empire, to its laws so wise, to its success on land, on sea and in commerce? In our confederation there will be catholics and protestants, English, French, Irish, Scotch, and each by its efforts and success will add to the prosperity of the dominion, to the glory of the new confederation. We are of different races, not to quarrel, but to work together for the common welfare. We cannot by law make the differences of race disappear, but I am convinced that the Anglo Canadians and the French Canadians will appreciate the advantages of their position. Set side by side, like a great family, their contact will produce a happy spirit of emulation. The diversity of races will in fact, believe me, contribute to the common prosperity.
That was the spirit of 1867, and that is the spirit of today. Indeed, when people tell me there are no developments taking place within our country toward the formation of a national purpose, I speak as one who on this day naturally looks back on his own lifetime. Who would have thought it possible that the day would come when a person of other than entirely British or French origin would be prime minister of this country? That would

have been a utopian dream; that would have been a figment of the imagination, but that is what has been brought about within this land. The divergencies of race and religion, while maintained constitutionally, none the less do not deny anyone within this land, whatever his origin, making his contribution to the country and having the support of all the people in endeavouring to do so.
That is the kind of Canada we are building. We are maintaining the rights under the constitution which must be inviolate and unchangeable, while at the same time bringing to this nation those of every race and religion, building a Canadianism. As I look back over my lifetime I see the tremendous change that has taken place. There is a new spirit of tolerance. There are some who say "Oh, we are divided east and west on the basis of race, origin and religion". I have not found that. I have found in my lifetime, and in particular since holding the responsible office that I hold today, that every part of this country, whatever its divergencies and differences may be, is united in a Canadianism and in a desire to build a strong, virile, vibrant and vital Canada.
I return now to the question of some of the things that might be done. While there will have to be diversification in the preparations -I am thinking of the capital city of Ottawa -we must keep other factors in mind. What are some of the things that have been suggested? In mentioning these I do not of course indicate that each and all of them will be accepted, but here are some of the suggestions that have been made.
One is the acceleration of the national capital plan. The next is the preservation of our historical monuments. I have dealt with this matter on previous occasions. One of our aims and purposes should be to preserve those places that are indeed the citadels of our freedom, that too often are removed or destroyed in order to meet the exigencies of modern life. One of those places is Earnscliffe, today the home of the British high commissioner in Canada. There indeed is one of those monuments that I hope in the years ahead will become part of the Canadian tradition and the property of the dominion. As one walks about in that place and sees the history of our country, one cannot help but have that feeling. One who has given strong support to that suggestion is the hon. member for Bona-vista-Twillingate. I refer to the necessity for the preservation of these things that, after all, show the greatness of a nation.
Then there has been suggested the establishment of a museum of Canadian history. Mention has been made of the greatness of our historical background. I await the day
Canadian Centennial
when a history will be written which is acceptable to all Canadians, representative of the greatness of our past, compiled by representatives of the two basic races and the other races to the end that no portion of the majesty of our past will be lost to the present and to the future. There has been the suggestion of a concert hall to make the nation's capital the artistic centre of Canada, to be taken in conjunction with the art gallery and those other institutions of art that we have within our city. The national library and the development of Sussex drive, along the lines that have been sketched and outlined by the Minister of Public Works, is a step in this direction. These are some of the things that will give substance to our national centennial and will also provide for Canadians yet unborn worthy and helpful institutions for the future. I return to one thing I have advocated throughout the years.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I wonder whether the Prime Minister would permit me to ask him one question before he goes on to this other point. I notice the Prime Minister did not mention a national auditorium. It seems to me-and recent events in Ottawa have made this very clear-that nothing is more needed than proper surroundings in which a national assembly could be held. This has been demonstrated by their lack in the last two or three years here in Ottawa.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR NATIONAL CORPORATION, NATIONAL CONFERENCE, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am glad to know that idea has just developed within the last two or three years. It is one of those things the need for which has become very apparent. It was not one of the matters that were brought to our direct attention as a result of the suggestions made, although there was a reference to a national convention headquarters. Certainly it would be possible I should think, for one of the institutions already mentioned to be used for the purposes the hon. member has in mind. I was about to mention once more the portable institution of the Canadian freedom train. The United States tried out this plan, I think some 15 years ago, and to every part of the union went a freedom train in which were kept the various charters of American freedom. The youth of the United States was thus privileged to see something of the greatness of its past and some of the foundations of American liberty. I hope that we in Canada may be able to secure from the United Kingdom some of the great charters of freedom that are ours, and that from France we may secure those declarations of the latter part of the eighteenth century-the declaration of the rights of man-and then the various other statutes of our own country which are part and parcel of our constitutional development,

National Housing Act
beginning with the Quebec Act which, as I said earlier today, provided for the first time in the history of what is today the commonwealth, for freedom of religion, in addition to the Constitutional Act, the Act of Union, the British North America Act, the Statute of Westminster and any other statutes and constitutional documents, including the bill of rights, habeas corpus and magna carta which are part of our heritage. Hon. members may realize that there is no copy of the British North America Act in an official form-that it was just a statute in the normal manner of the passage of statutes through the United Kingdom parliament. Our foundation instrument is not an attractive one in the sense of its decorative or artistic qualities but it does represent something and there is a copy available which would be of great interest to the people of our country.
I do not think there is anything further I wish to say at this time except once again to bespeak the co-operation of hon. members and of the people of Canada as a whole so that when the organization is set up it may be said of us, in the words quoted by the hon. member for Queens which appear in the room in which the fathers of confederation met in Charlottetown, as it was said of them: "They builded better than they knew".
Resolution reported and concurred in.
Mr. Diefenbaker thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. C-127 respecting the observance of the centennial of confederation in Canada.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING AMOUNTS AVAILABLE FOR LOANS AND RESEARCH
speechtext:
Because of the sincere and continuing interest of all hon. members in the question of housing, I propose at this time to make what might otherwise be considered as a somewhat comprehensive statement to the best of my ability so that I may anticipate some of the questions which must be in the minds of many of us after the summer recess.
Housing is a subject which has in a great measure been above party politics during the time I have been minister. All members of the house, in accordance with their own points of view, have made efforts to contribute toward the provision of better housing for our people and I know that everyone, regardless of where he sits, will be happy to know that since June, 1957, a new dwelling unit-a house or apartment-has been completed virtually every minute of every working day during the four year period.
The provision of new housing at this spectacular and unprecedented rate is, I respectfully suggest, an accomplishment in which each of us can take just pride. It is an accomplishment which we can better appreciate when we measure it in terms of human beings-hundreds of thousands of Canadian families obtaining new homes, many for the first time, or at least moving to a new and better environment in which to live and nurture their children. It is an accomplishment, too, which clearly indicates the forthright, considered and, if I may say so, successful approach by this government to a vital social and economic problem of national proportions. It is also interesting to know that there are today two million Canadians living in new homes-homes which were not built when this government took office four years ago.
Of the housing accommodation built since 1957, 42.6 per cent, or very close to one-half, was financed under the National Housing Act and, in turn, approximately one-half of the N.H.A. total was constructed with direct federal government assistance. To put it in another way, more than 595,000 new dwelling units have been built during the past four and a half years, of which some 252,000 were financed under the National Housing Act; and of the N.H.A. content, more than 132,000

units were made possible through the medium of public mortgage funds aggregating $1,264.9 million.
This, of course, is only a part of the story and I shall, if I may, deal with some of the other aspects a little later in my remarks. I shall be very happy to answer any questions asked by hon. members and to receive their suggestions as to how we can better go forward to build what we hope will be a magnificent program in housing. Meanwhile, Mr. Chairman, perhaps I may be permitted to review very briefly the situation that faced us in 1960, the positive actions taken by the government and the reflection of these actions in the results attained.
Hon. members may recall that on November 22, 1960-it seems so long ago when this session began; on that occasion I believe I had the privilege of introducing the first measure of the session-in introducing another measure to amend the National Housing Act, I said:
For the first time since the war demand for housing has become a limiting factor.
There were good reasons for the pause. The pressures of population and income growth had abated and the sustained rate of building in the post-war years had greatly improved general housing conditions. But it was a pause and I believe I was careful to stress that we considered it to be nothing more than that, a rest for revaluation, a time to take stock ourselves.
Our assessment, which events are already showing to be a valid one, was based on general acceptance of the fact that a very real need for good housing still exists, especially for the lower income groups, and will continue to exist for many years to come. But as 1960 advanced, it became increasingly apparent that we were undergoing a transition, a transition from 15 years of active, unbroken demand to an anticipated period of marked improvement throughout most of this decade when the children born in the years following the war will reach maturity and enter the housing market.
There were of course many problems accompanying the transition, problems that required a hard day to day scrutiny of our housing policies. As a result new measures geared to meet changing conditions were enacted from time to time by parliament and our administrative arrangements which are designed for a maximum of flexibility were also revised as required.
During last fall several other measures were introduced to stimulate winter construction and to encourage the highest possible level of employment in the building trades. These included a reduced rate of interest
National Housing Act
on loans to limited dividend companies providing rental accommodation for lower income families and for elderly persons; and extension of home improvement loans to rental properties including apartment houses. I need hardly say that these measures have had a tremendous influence on the house building industry in this past year.
The importance of housing to the economy was given further emphasis in December,
1960,	when a major rejuvenation of the National Housing Act was effected. Parliament passed a number of amendments which gave the act new purpose and which today are having far reaching consequences for the nation as well as for the housing industry. As a matter of fact we are very pleased to have noted that as Canada worked its way out of the recession it was the housing industry directed by the government which led the way.
Hon. members will recall, for instance, that the ratio of loan to lending value was increased to provide higher loans and lower down payments; the maximum National Housing Act loan by regulation was raised; the permissive repayment period was extended to 35 years; funds available by statute for redevelopment of the blighted areas of our cities were doubled to $50 million; the federal-provincial partnership arrangements were widened to permit the acquisition and renovation of existing lands for public housing.
In addition, of course, two completely new concepts were introduced into the National Housing Act, federal assistance to municipalities to finance the construction of sewage treatment projects and to universities to provide living accommodation for resident students.
What have been the results of these perceptive, imaginative actions? What has happened as a result of the government's determination to stand by every bona fide home owner applicant and any builder who has a purchaser?
I can tell the committee that while the value of contract awards in the business, industrial and engineering fields declined by about 10 per cent, 15 per cent and 25 per cent respectively during the first seven months of
1961,	residential contract awards jumped by some 30 per cent. These are remarkable figures to contemplate, but it is patent that new house construction and, in turn, new employment opportunities would also have suffered materially had activity not been spearheaded by an effective, up to date National Housing Act in the passing of which measure all hon. members of this committee shared.

National Housing Act
systems are being provided where they did not exist before. Furthermore, construction of sewage systems in the smaller localities has, in many instances, encouraged the installation of public water systems to replace individual wells.
Now, federal sewage loans have also enabled many major centres to extend their trunk sewage systems and either enlarge or, where none existed, establish sewage treatment plants. Sewage disposal and treatment have as one of their objectives the prevention of damage to receiving waters. The damage that may be done includes contamination or pollution of water supplies, bathing places and fishing grounds. This all-out effort by municipalities, in conjunction with the other levels of government, will do much to free our rivers, streams, lakes and coastal waters of the pollution problem. I should like, at this point, to commend the city of Ottawa for its foresight and for the promptness with which it acted to avail itself of the opportunities under the National Housing Act to go ahead immediately with its tremendous sewage disposal plant. The mayor of Ottawa deserves a great deal of credit for her leadership in this regard.
Since the legislation received royal assent on December 2, I960, we have already approved 106 loans to municipalities in every province in Canada. In addition, 14 other formal applications are being processed which will mean more than $44 million of the $100 million provided by statute for this purpose will have been allocated. There are also 203 preliminary inquiries, representing a loan potential of $70 million, on hand so that by early next year the entire $100 million should be committed.
The amendment the committee is being asked to consider would have the effect of increasing the statutory vote for funds for municipal sewage treatment project loans to $200 million from $100 million.
I now come to loans to universities to assist in the construction of accommodation for full-time students in the form of either new residences or the conversion of existing buildings into dormitories. This is the subject of another amendment to the National Housing Act now being recommended. To qualify under the N.H.A., as hon. members are aware, this type of accommodation must consist primarily of bedrooms and sanitary facilities, although dining halls and lounges will be considered in the over-all picture. Other facilities necessary to operate the project, such as self contained family housing units for the senior supervisor of resident students and a caretaker, may also be provided. Loan amounts are based on 90 per cent of the cost of the project, subject to a maximum of $7,000 for each student accommo-

dated. Loans may be for a term of up to 50 years and their interest at a rate prescribed by the governor in council, as low a rate as is possible.
The provision of dormitories for universities was a problem of national concern. The increasing number of scholarships, bursaries and grants has lowered many of the economic barriers to a university education and has contributed to an unprecedented rise in enrolment. All hon. members are interested in seeing that children, if they are properly qualified, have an opportunity for university education. Let us look at these figures: 63,500 enrolled in universities in 1952, 114,000 are enrolled at the present time and the estimate for our centenary year, 1967, is 185,000. This enrolment is increasing at a tremendous rate. The national conference of Canadian universities reported in 1958 that 60 per cent of all full-time students were domiciled 15 or more miles away from the university. Resident accommodation was limited to 25 per cent of the student body. Those of you who have attended university and have been unable to gain admittance to one of the university residences can appreciate the problems students are having at the present time.
Construction of adequate dormitories on university campuses will accomplish two purposes: First, those who travel many miles each day to obtain an education will be able to move to the university grounds, with its attendant benefits; and those living in small towns who heretofore have been denied an education because of lack of accommodation will now be able to attend university.
Response by the universities to these long term, low interest loans has been most gratifying and the program is achieving unqualified success. To date, applications for loans have been received from 30 universities and colleges and an additional 23 have made preliminary inquiries. Sixteen loans in the amount of $18 million have already been approved. Approvals and applications on hand will result in loans totalling more than $35 million. These would provide accommodation for in excess of 7,800 resident students.
Now, to avoid the possibility of running out of commitment authority-you will recall that when I became minister in the summer of 1959 we were either running out or had run out of commitment authority as the hon. member for Nipissing will recall-it is recommended that this statutory vote be increased to $100 million from $50 million.
The fourth and final proposed amendment, Mr. Chairman, relates to part V of the National Housing Act. Under part V, a responsibility is imposed upon Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to provide leadership in the search for a house of more beauty,

a house of greater utility for Canadians at a lower cost; in other words, a better home for less money. This is what we all want, a better home for less money. Sections 32 and 33 of the National Housing Act enumerate 15 items of a general nature to which the corporation is to give its attention. It is under this part of the act, for example, that provision is made for scholarships, bursaries and urban renewal studies. As minister, I have been amazed at the great interest manifested in better housing as the result of the encouragement of these scholarships and bursaries and the urban renewal studies provided by the government.
Section 35 of the National Housing Act contains a statutory vote of $5 million for these purposes. This amount has been almost fully committed. It is now recommended that the statutory vote of $5 million should be increased to $10 million. This will restore the commitment authority to the amount originally provided by the act.
That briefly is the scope of the new housing legislation we are seeking at this time and the reasons additional commitment authority is required on these four counts. May I just summarize:	First, an increase of
$500 million in the statutory appropriation provided by section 22 of the National Housing Act to $2 billion; second, an increase of $100 million in the statutory vote under section 36H(3) to $200 million; third, an increase of $50 million in the statutory vote under section 36GC2) to $100 million; and fourth, an increase of $5 million in the statutory vote under section 35 to $10 million.
In concluding my remarks, Mr. Chairman, may I ask the indulgence of hon. members for a few minutes more in order to review one or two other considerations which the committee may want me to touch upon at this time.
My remarks have indicated that house building has not been impeded in 1961 by any over-all shortage of mortgage funds for National Housing Act lending. It must be remembered, however, that this year 40 per cent of all National Housing Act loans have been made by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation-and I know the hon. member for Nipissing particularly will want to know this-with funds provided by the government and that private funds for National Housing Act lending have been quite inadequate to meet the total demand for National Housing Act loans. Hon. members of the House of Commons have heard me say over and over again how anxious we are to have more and more private funds finance this great program of national building in order to relieve the government of the necessity of doing so in as great an amount as we
National Housing Ace
are doing at the present time. But this year, in order to meet the commitments the government, through Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, has made contributions up to 40 per cent of all the National Housing Act loans made this year so that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, in its role as residual lender will likely make loans up to $300 million.
This does not mean that the National Housing Act interest rate cannot be reduced as long as Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation is engaged in the lending business. This question about the interest rate is asked very often. No one is more interested in it than am I. On the other hand, there would be little point in lowering the National Housing Act interest rate-and I ask all hon. members to note this point-if the principal effect of such a change were to replace private funds with government funds in the National Housing Act market, particularly since the government already is committed to 40 per cent of National Housing Act lending this year.
It has always been the policy of this government to maintain the lowest possible National Housing Act interest rate that would attract a substantial flow of mortgage funds for housing. Hon. members will recall that the National Housing Act provides for a ceiling N.H.A. interest rate 2J per cent higher than the interest rate on long term federal government bonds. This government has been able to encourage a substantial flow of mortgage funds from the private lenders at a rate significantly lower than the maximum provided in the National Housing Act. If a new National Housing Act interest rate were prescribed today, the formula contained in the National Housing Act would permit-and I ask the hon. member for Nipissing to note this point-a maximum rate of 7J per cent but, notwithstanding the attractiveness of alternative investments, such as corporate bonds and provincial and municipal bonds, the government has been able to hold the National Housing Act rate at 6j per cent. The government will continue its efforts to maintain the National Housing Act interest rate at the lowest possible level. This matter is subject to continuous review, and the National Housing Act rate will be reduced as soon as the relative attractiveness of this rate as compared with other investment yields will permit the action to be taken, without impeding the flow of mortgage funds for housing purposes. Even with a rate of 6J per cent we are only able to get this year from private lenders a 60 per cent participation in National Housing Act lending.
I therefore ask hon. members not to worry about my attention to the interest rate. I

National Housing Act
think about it every month and indeed every week. We have had our review. We have many reviews. I am always saying, "When can we reduce the interest rate?" However, until long term government bond-and my hon. friends know what I mean-yields are reduced, this cannot be done. As hon. members can appreciate, if the bonds go up in price, the interest rate gets correspondingly less. As soon as we reduce those bonds, just so soon will we be able to reduce the N.H.A. interest rate on loans for houses.
May I now say a word about assistance to lower income families. This is a matter close to my heart because, as all hon. members know, I am interested in this subject inasmuch as in my riding of Rosedale we have the first huge federal-provincial development located in Regent park. I am therefore vitally interested in lower income families. In the first place, the more generous N.H.A. terms afforded by statute in December last have a direct bearing on the amount of mortgage loan available, the amount of down payments required and the length of time over which the loan may be repaid. The easier terms are there, of course, for any prospective borrower who is eligible, but it must be obvious that the greatest advantage is to families of modest means and it was this group we had very much in mind when we sought from parliament last year authority to make these important statutory revisions.
I would point out also, that this year so far 36.3 per cent of National Housing Act borrowers have had annual incomes of $5,000 or less.
Second, I must point to the very heavy volume of lending under the limited dividend provisions of the act to assist in financing rental accommodation for families who come from the lower third income group in their community and also limited dividend projects built for elderly persons. Again, as I do every time I make a speech to these wonderful charitable and service clubs across Canada, I commend the taking of cognizance of the opportunity for service in their communities by building in their communities under their aegis, direction and control, limited dividend projects. They will not lose any money in the long run. The government will put up 90 per cent of the funds; they put up 10 per cent of them. The cost is amortized over a period of 40 years at a low interest rate. They can be of great benefit to the people in the lower income bracket and to the elderly people in their community by doing a service of this kind.
To September 8 of this year loans have been approved for nearly 3,000 units of this kind, a figure that compares with 510 units for the same period of 1960. Just think about that. It is almost six times as many and it is

almost double the total for all of that year. The value of limited dividend loans approved this year to date is $22.9 million, against $3 million a year ago.
Third, since this government took office in 1957 more than 3,000 units of federal-provincial housing have been approved under section 36 of the National Housing Act to a value of $34 million. This is equivalent to one half of all federal-provincial housing approved by the previous government since the measure was introduced in 1949. Again, federal-provincial housing is intended for lower income families. Indeed, in September, 1960 the average tenant had an income of $3,288 per year.
Finally, grants in an estimated amount of $13.5 million have been made by the federal government for slum clearance purposes since 1957, a little more than double the amount made available by the previous government, and there can be no doubt that this assistance ultimately is of the greatest possible help to families of lesser means.
All these beneficial provisions of the National Housing Act, together with the many helpful services afforded by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to the public and to prospective home owners, suggest on the part of the government, I think hon. members will agree, a very high degree of interest in and of assistance to the lower income family. But I can assure you, Mr. Chairman, that no assistance which we can render can be great enough.
I wish to say something about the 35-year repayment period. Hon. members will recall that we extended the period, but we only do this where it is a case of necessity and where we ascertain that the person who receives such an extension is readily qualified and otherwise would not be able to obtain a loan.
I now wish to refer to the mortgage insurance fund. I expect to hear some remarks from the hon. member for Nipissing about this. It is one of his favourite subjects and I am always glad to hear from him on it.

speechtext:
Thank you very much, Mr. Chairman, and through you hon. members of the committee. I have almost completed my remarks. As of July 31, 1961 the assets of the mortgage insurance fund totalled $79.1

million against mortgage loans outstanding of more than $3,428 million. The assets included $793,760 in mortgages, $4,062,625 in real estate, close to $1 million in accrued interest and the balance in cash or government securities. From March, 1954, when mortgage insurance was introduced, to September 13, 1961, 835 claims were made against the fund and the value of claims paid was in excess of $7.8 million.
Thus, although our loss experience to date has not been unduly severe, he would be a very rash man indeed who would seriously counsel against maintaining, and continuing to increase, our insurance against losses of public funds that are outstanding in such large amounts.
I wish to say just a word about the secondary mortgage market. Again, I stress that we are not talking about second mortgages, but about the secondary mortgage market. As hon. members know, a second successful offering of National Housing Act insured loans was made in August. The auction resulted in a wider list of successful bidders, together with first use of the 60-day option arrangement.
As announced on August 30, total bids and requests for options in the amount of $21 million were received for the $17.5 million offering, of which not more than $15 million was to be sold. The value of accepted tenders was $9.75 million, bringing to $22.25 million aggregate sales for the June and August auctions. In addition, there were accepted requests for options in August for $3.75 million.
The average accepted tender price was 101.35, compared with 101.17 for the initial offering made in June. Bids were again received from chartered banks, life insurance and trust companies and investment dealers.
We are very much encouraged by results of the offerings for two reasons. First, their success indicates a growing interest on the part of those whom we would expect to develop a secondary market in mortgages, and we now know that a number of loans purchased in June have since been resold to Canadian pension funds, some of which had not previously invested in mortgages. On the basis of our experience to date we expect a third offering will be made during the next few months. We are criticized at times for not offering a larger amount at these auctions. After all, we want to test the market and we want to develop this secondary mortgage market in an orderly and sensible way.
Mr. Chairman, those are my remarks on this resolution. I should be very happy to hear not only advice from hon. members of the committee, but also any constructive criticism.
National Housing Act
There is no one more anxious than I, as the minister in charge of the department and responsible for reporting to parliament in connection with Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, to find ways and means of developing our concept of having every Canadian properly housed.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING AMOUNTS AVAILABLE FOR LOANS AND RESEARCH
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, before dealing directly with the resolution I should like to take this opportunity to draw the attention of hon. members to the fact that national home week began last Saturday. I know that builders and the many others engaged in the house building industry will be putting forth extra efforts during this national home week. New models and new ideas for better living will be on display, in many cases for the first time, in an effort to reach today's home buyer, who is becoming more and more selective. The prospective buyer today is doing more shopping than ever before in his search for better value for his money.
I should like to pay tribute to those many Canadians engaged in the house building industry, to the people concerned in construction and selling, and in fact to all who are connected with this industry. I believe the great majority of the people engaged in this important industry are continually searching for ways and means of improving their particular field and in so doing are making a worthwhile contribution to the never ending job of providing better housing for Canadians.
I should like first of all to thank the minister for his very comprehensive and, if I may say so-I do not want him to misunderstand me-lengthy statement. He has covered the field very thoroughly. In fact, he has covered the actions of his government for the past four years since they took office. My remarks today, on the contrary, will be rather brief as we on this side of the chamber await the bill itself and the examination of it which will be made later.
I believe the outstanding aspect of the legislation which will follow today's resolution will be found in the timing of the legislation and the tremendous sums involved, especially in the light of the statements of the Prime Minister, that the next election will be fought on the basis of free enterprise v. socialism.
This legislation-at least that portion of it that increases the amount of $1,500 million to $2,000 million for direct lending-shows the degree to which this government has become involved in financing home construction. Despite their many statements that they intend to resume a residual role in this field, this legislation, necessary though it may be at this time, points up the degree to which

National Housing Act this government has taken over from the private sector. I intend to say more on this subject a little later on.
The other outstanding feature of the proposed legislation is the fact that it ignores completely the real problem that faces the prospective home buyer today. I refer to the high cost of housing resulting from the high interest rates which have been made necessary and which are being maintained, apparently, under this government despite their protests to the contrary. We, as members of this committee, must satisfy ourselves that the amount envisaged in the first section of this proposed legislation is justified at this time. We must ask ourselves: does this government really intend to lend this money in the near future or are they simply seeking to provide election insurance? I was hoping the minister would have been more specific-that he would have taken this house and the country into his confidence to a greater extent concerning the government's intentions for the next year or more. Perhaps there will be an opportunity for the minister to do that later on.
The legislation envisaged in this resolution, as the hon. gentleman has pointed out, falls into four distinct categories. While we are in basic agreement with the principle of the resolution just as we were in December when somewhat similar legislation was before us, and while we do not intend to offer any obstacle to its passage, we do believe that the first item

the increase from $1.5 billion to $2 billion-is worthy of some examination. However, before dealing with the first section may I say we warmly support sections 2, 3 and 4. That more research and community planning is required there will be no argument in this house. With respect to the third and fourth items dealing with loans for university housing projects and municipal sewage treatment projects, I may say that we are in full accord, as we were last December. However, as we said then, and especially in the case of the sewage treatment section, we did not feel the government's proposals went far enough. We believe there is a great need by our hard pressed municipalities for a much larger degree of assistance such as could be provided by a municipal loan fund along the lines we have been recommending since 1958.
We hope the increase in the ceiling from $1.5 billion to $2 billion will assure that in the future the government will not make the same mistake as it did between October 1959 and April 1960-the mistake of not making needed funds available, with the consequent disastrous impact on housing staffs during the first half of 1960 and the resulting substantial loss of employment opportunities at a time when they were needed most. The low level of starts last year-108,858, the lowest


since 1953-provides the statistical basis for government claims of an increase in 1961 as compared with last year's starts. I would also point out that the low carry-over of houses under construction has resulted in completions between January and July, 1961, being 18.4 per cent less than in the same period of 1960. In these circumstances over-all activity in residential construction has shown, really, only marginal improvement. We are perhaps justified in pointing out in passing that in respect to the legislation approved only last December the fact that the government is now asking for further increases raises some doubt as to the ability of this administration to plan ahead.
The first increase-the increase from $1.5 billion to $2 billion-is interesting in view of the government's oft-professed role as the only champions of free enterprise. It is of interest to note that during the last three full years of Liberal administration-1954, 1955 and 1956-approximately 380,000 homes were started as opposed to the 415,000 during the three full years of Tory administration, 1958, 1959 and 1960. The Liberal administration of those days found it necessary to lend only $65 million, while direct loans from 1958 to 1960 amounted to $924 million. In other words, in order to build less than 10 per cent more houses this government had to increase its lending by approximately 1,400 per cent; to start 35,000 more houses in three full years they had to supply $860 million more from the public sector. This is some example of free enterprise.
I should like to say just a few words with respect to the outlook of the future. Despite the fact that in July housing starts were below those of July last year-8,682 as against 8,966-and that on a seasonally adjusted basis starts have been tending downward since March, I believe there is every indication that during the next 12 months housing starts could recover substantially from last year's low level. Demand for housing, in the sense that there are still many Canadians who are ill housed, continues to be very great. However, there must always be the fear that as general economic conditions improve, as the recovery from recession broadens and, in particular, if a mild expansion should take place during the next 12 months that the government may once again lose interest in the housing industry or, conversely, in an election year, overstimulate that industry. Wise policy and planning is required. Often in the past over-emphasis of the anti-cyclical aspect of house building or over-stimulation of the industry has resulted in feast or famine situations, with an obvious upward pressure on the cost of housing. On previous occasions we have

dealt in some detail with the increase in costs and the fact that in consequence builders are unable to carry out any long term planning. It is not my intention to review those points today.
I should like, now, to say a few words about demand. Interest rates are one of the major factors because, as hon. members know, home owners are the largest users of long term credit. High interest rates have added and are adding substantially to the resistance of prospective buyers. Yet, as has been shown during the past few years, governments do have a tremendous influence on interest rates through both fiscal and monetary policies. We all recognize the control that any federal government has over interest rates by its power to adjust National Housing Act interest rates. It is my view, expressed at every opportunity and perhaps, in the minds of some, too often, that the main deterrent to the development of a more vigorous housing industry during these past many months have been this government's stubborn insistence on maintaining high interest rates. The rate of 6| per cent represents the highest ever during the life of the National Housing Act. I should like to cite one example, that of chartered banks. They have played a very important role during most of the time since they were introduced into the housing business in the time of the previous administration. It should be recalled that as recently as 1958 the chartered banks lent over $300 million. Well, this government maintained a high interest rate of 6| per cent, keeping the banks out of lending for housing during these past two years. I can think of few investments more attractive to the bank than these gilt-edged government backed mortgages at 6 per cent, yet this government keeps the banks out of approved lending by maintaining an N.H.A. rate of 6j per cent.
Finally, I should like to make a brief comment on the secondary mortgage market, which has been recommended from this side of the house for the past three years. We believe the government should be giving some consideration to the establishment of a federal agency which would purchase N.H.A. guaranteed mortgages and use them as collateral against the issuance of certificates in small denominations which would be made available to small investors.
During the last decade innumerable innovations have been perfected by those competing for the nation's savings. One has but to recall the gimmicks incorporated in the conversion loan to show to what lengths efforts have gone to create new instruments to attract funds. National Housing Act

As I say, before any intelligent work was done on that design it was duplicated a hundred thousand times across the country. During election time I have had occasion to visit many thousands of suburban dwellings, and in almost every case the design is such that if a fourth living area is desired on the ground floor it requires in effect turning an existing bedroom into a hallway to reach it. This is one of the fundamental challenges to the architectural profession and leads, of course, to planning the lot, the design and other factors. I think this would be high on the list and I put forward the suggestion that scholarships and bursaries be focused on trying to find a solution to that problem.

In my view the ideal would be the erection of smaller units sprinkled among the suburban population rather than the large and in most cases more efficient units in institutions which have a tendency sometimes to identify the area and preclude the kind of social intercourse that is desired between the senior citizen and the younger people with younger families in those growing communities. National Housing Act

I should like to take a minute to make an observation on the housing program with particular reference to the low rental housing. I understand that low rental housing is made available to people within a certain range of income and that in computing the family income the family allowance

payments are included. This was brought to my attention this summer when a number of veterans exceeded the income bracket for two reasons. In one case the pension plus the earnings had put him over the ceiling and, in the other case, the ceiling had been exceeded by reason of the inclusion of the family allowance payment.
It seems to me that there is a principle here at which we would do well to take another look. It does not seem right to me that family allowance payments should be counted as income for the purposes of this act. Family allowance payments, as I understand them, are paid to the parents to insure the well being of the children; they are not meant to be used for housing or for general expenditures and should not be counted as part of the general family income. There is another side to this question because such action penalizes the large family. In other words, if there are two or three children in the family, the family can probably stay within the prescribed income bracket, but if the family consists of a large number of children then receipt of family allowance payments puts that family beyond the ceiling and they have to look for another home. Making eligibility dependent upon the number of children is a principle, I think, that deserves to be reconsidered and I would ask the minister to reconsider this policy of including family allowance payments in computing income under the National Housing Act.

My only reason for rising this afternoon is the question asked by the hon. member for Nipissing of the hon. member for York-Scarborough. Certainly, last year this government ran out of funds but only after having put forward $300 million for housing last year. Then, the government brought forward further funds and made it $500 million.
All I am asking hon. members to do is to compare this amount with the rather puny start made by the Liberal government in 1954 under this act. They made available a total of $150 million. As I say, last year we put forward $300 million, then added $500 million and now we are putting forward another $500 million. In my opinion, the laughable part of the whole situation is the fact that although the Liberals put forward $150 million in 1954, by 1957 only $100 million of these funds had been put into housing. The

ridiculous part of this whole argument is that in 1957 the building of homes in Canada was at a standstill. What was the reason for this situation? The Liberal government brought in a true tight money policy. In other words, they upped the reserve from 8 per cent to 15 per cent and they stopped loans under the National Housing Act. This is the truth.
Look at your own constituency. In my constituency there were only one or two houses being built under the National Housing Act at that time. Ever since this party came into power we have been building more and more houses throughout the constituency. Under the present Conservative government policy, money has been made available, and that is all there is to it. Let us look at those figures again. Under the Liberals, $150 million were made available and only $100 million were allocated. Compare those figures with the figures for the present day. I believe about $2 billion-I may be wrong and it may be more-have been made available for housing.
The implication in my friend's question about running out is that this government could not look far enough ahead. We have looked ahead and we have provided funds at a time when they have been required for housing in Canada. As the most junior member of the opposition may I join in the cordial felicitations to the Prime Minister on this happy occasion of his birthday. I sincerely wish him a long and happy life crowded with pleasure and leisure.
I will not congratulate the minister on any particular phase of his program because such congratulations would tend to be repetitive of what he himself has said so enthusiastically. The hon. member for York-Scarborough has repeated almost each word of praise. However, I would say this to the minister. Even in the short time I have been in the house, I have become cognizant of the fact that he has been' willing to redress little matters of grievance. I should therefore like to mention briefly, if I may, with respect it this legislation some matters to which I think it would he helpful for him to address himself.
Both the minister and the hon. member for York-Scarborough, as I understand it, live in Toronto. The type of riding I represent is very different from those which they represent. This summer I took some time to fly over my riding of Leeds and study it from the air. I could not fail to be impressed by the comparative congestion of the town of Brock-ville and the town of Gananoque with the relatively uncrowded villages. A village like Elgin, for example, which has an extremely fine school, could grow and develop with some sort of assistance. Lansdowne and Athens are two other places that could easily develop with adequate assistance. The town of Smiths Falls which spills into the riding of Leeds to the south must grow in that direction. These places are in my opinion, of the type that could be given some interested scrutiny by the minister.
A riding such as Leeds, which is half urban and half rural, compels certain comparisons. I have been made aware of the fact that our farm population has been declining for approximately 20 years. Not only is that the fact, but these very attractive villages which were to a certain extent the centre of culture some years ago and which were happy places in which to live, have declined in importance rather than grown. I would ask the minister to consider the extent to which this legislation could be made applicable to some of these areas on the fringe of our towns or even in the smaller areas.
My constituents have made me cognizant of the fact that federal housing assistance appears to be available to the town dweller but

not to the country dweller and of the fact that in this regard there is marked disparity. It would be improper within the confines of this debate to spill over into the responsibilities, for example, of the Minister of Agriculture under the Farm Credit Act. However, I think it would be fair to say this. So much red tape is attendant upon getting farm loans that we must perhaps look to our Minister of Public Works for as liberal, broad and generous interpretation as is possible of the provisions of this act.
By people interested in housing and in construction, particularly in the Brockville area, it has been brought to my attention that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation was at first brought into being to promote home building in areas that were unserviced and therefore not acceptable to insurance companies. It was for the purpose of issuing loans to individuals who perhaps could not qualify for insurance company loans. If I am in error in understanding the origins of this act, I am sure I will be corrected. However, in 1961 in the Kingston area we have seen a sharp change with respect to this approach. Now we find rulings which provide that no lot, unless it has services or is in a C.M.H.C. approved subdivision, is acceptable for a C.M.H.C. loan. This, to the thinking of some people very much interested in construction today, would appear to place C.M.H.C. in direct competition with the insurance companies, leaving the former field in which we understand C.M.H.C. was originally particularly interested with no one to look after it.
It seems almost as though in the C.M.H.C. Kingston area a circle has been drawn around a certain point in each town and at various distances out from the limits anyone beyond the perimeter is able to build on his land-for example, with septic systems, septic tanks and tank installations-but beyond that point this is not possible. I of course understand how the minister, whose program involves so many millions of dollars, is urgently concerned about orderly urban development. I can quite appreciate that lack of discipline and lack of orderly growth in this regard could be harmful and damaging. On the other hand I suggest to the minister that there are, particularly in a riding such as mine-which is on the river and extends to the north-many areas which have not been developed at all.
There are places such as Lyndhurst, Elgin, Morton, Delta, and so on, where the persons who live in those villages are for the most part employed in the towns. Many people work in Smiths Falls, Kingston or Brockville and there is not much difference between our countryfolk and our townsfolk. These

are not farmers; they are people enjoying a sort of suburban life. Before the minister simply rejects this suggestion I ask him to consider the possibility of liberalizing to some extent the conditions and requirements of these loans. Every area of ground is different, as we know. There is the problem of sewerage. They are working toward improvement in Gananoque at the present time. I must speak appreciatively of this aspect of assistance to our urban areas.
The Minister of Finance has visited our area. On one occasion in Athens he spoke on behalf of the late Hayden Stanton regarding the requirement of municipalities for greater assistance. This extremely well attended meeting was held in 1957 and his promise of municipal assistance was well received by people who knew something about the burden of municipal financing in our county. I think our municipalities are in a somewhat worse condition today than they were when the Minister of Finance made those suggestions in respect of the assistance to be provided.
The matter of assistance with respect to sewage disposal is of vital importance to an area such as Gananoque. We have there a community of 5,000 people who at the present moment are embarking upon a sewerage plan which will probably cost them in the order of $605,000. Without assistance it will be quite impossible for them to carry out this project. It will mean an expense of $121 for every man, woman and child in that small town, which has suffered its share of unemployment in the past two years. I think federal assistance for sewerage development is vitally important.
I also put forward this other point which I hope the minister will appreciate. problem by all sorts of means. But we, of the Conservative government, have each year taken steps to help the population and create increased employment opportunities.

I think the fact that the minister has brought in this resolution to amend the National Housing Act so as to make more funds available is in itself an indication that a need still exists. Certainly, no member of this committee would quarrel with the fact that, within a period of less than a year since last December when this legislation was previously amended so as to provide for university housing projects, it should be necessary to double the amount of money available. This only emphasizes the great need which existed in that area. When we find that the legislation brought in last December providing for assistance to municipalities in respect to sewerage projects has now to be amended so as to double the amount available, I think that sufficiently answers the question whether or not there was a need in that direction.
I wish to compliment the Department of Public Works and its minister on the fact that they have so greatly enlarged the degree of assistance given to communities whose population is less than 5,000. In my own community this assistance has led to its virtually doubling in size. Leduc, which is outside the international airport, has built this year nearly 100 homes, which represent about 25 per cent of its previous size. My own city of Wetaskiwin has had the largest percentage increase in building of any city in Alberta- an increase of 186 per cent. This, of course, is due in part to the fact that our population has increased as a result of a new Carnation milk plant coming into the city and also because of the fact that we shall be an alternate headquarters for the military establishment in Edmonton, as the Minister of National Defence announced the other day. Both in Ponoka and Rimbey there have been substantial increases in housing accommodation, and all this has happened just in the last couple of years since the act was broadened to include the smaller centres.
One thing I would urge on the minister and his department: I suggest they should seriously consider reserving a greater portion of these funds which are now being made available for the provision of smaller homes at lower cost. This would provide the lower income groups with more opportunities of buying homes than they have at the present

speakeroldname: Mr. Richard A. Bell (Parliamentary Secre-iary to the Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: LEGISLATION RESPECTING ADMINISTRATION OF WESTERN SCHOOL LANDS
speechtext:
The purpose of the bill to be founded upon this resolution is to secure parliamentary approval of agreements which have been entered into between the government of Canada and the governments of the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta. These agreements were laid on the table of the house on the 15th of this month by the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Halpenny) and they appear as schedules to the bill. If approved by parliament and by the legislatures of the respective provinces, these agreements will have the effect of terminating the legislative control of the parliament of Canada over the school lands and school lands funds of the three prairie provinces and placing the administration and disposal of those lands and funds within the sole competence of the respective legislatures of those provinces.
The committee may wish to have recalled some of the historical background of the school lands and school lands funds. Under the Dominion Lands Act of 1872, the parliament of Canada set aside two sections of land 90205-6-536J
in each township in Manitoba and the then Northwest Territories as an endowment for education and in the consolidated Dominion Lands Act of 1879 set forth the manner in which this endowment was to be administered by the department of the interior. All sales were to be made by public auction after due advertisement, and at an upset price based upon the fair value of other unoccupied lands in the township. The terms of sale, which have subsequently been changed from time to time, were fixed in 1879 at one fifth in cash and the remainder in nine annual instalments with interest at 6 per cent. The principal arising from the sales was to be invested in dominion securities and the interest arising therefrom as well as the annual revenue from leases, hay permits, etc., on school lands were, after deducting the cost of management of the lands, to be paid annually to the governments of the province or territory within which such lands were situated. The moneys so paid were to be used by the province or territory to support public schools in such manner as the province or territory deemed expedient. In conformity with the above requirements, the government of Canada from 1883, the date of the first sale of school lands, until 1930, when the school lands and school lands funds were transferred to the jurisdiction of the provinces in the natural resources settlement of that year, administered the school lands and school lands funds.
In the agreements which constituted the 1930 natural resources settlement, the three provinces undertook to administer the school lands and the school lands fund they acquired in the settlement, according to the provisions of sections 37 to 40 of the Dominion Lands Act, being chapter 113 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1927. This provision of the natural resources agreements meant that while the provinces had assumed the administration of their school lands and associated funds, the principles on which those lands and funds were to be administered were not to change. The provinces were required to invest the principal from the sale of school lands in a school lands fund and invest the moneys of the fund in securities of Canada.
There have over the years been various representations from one or more of the prairie provinces to have the provisions of the natural resources transfer agreements of 1930 dealing with school lands and the school lands funds amended. As the result of such representations the natural resources transfer agreement with Saskatchewan was amended

Western School Lands Administration in 1948 and in 1951 the transfer agreements with each of the three provinces was amended. The 1948 amendment allowed Saskatchewan to sell school lands to veterans under provisions of the Veterans' Land Act without conforming to the requirement that school lands must only be sold at public auction. The 1951 amendment gave the provinces more latitude as to the securities in which the school lands funds might be invested. The definition of acceptable securities was broadened to include, in addition to securities of Canada, securities of any province, or securities of a municipal corporation or school districts within the province together with securities guaranteed by Canada or a province.
There have been since that time various representations from the prairie provinces that all federal legislative control over their school lands and school lands funds should be removed and the legislatures of the provinces given sole jurisdiction as to the manner of administration or disposal of the lands and the funds. It has been argued that the revenues provided from the school lands are now small in relation to total expenditures on education so that it can scarcely be contended that the maintenance of the funds assures adequate revenues for education.
I have in my hand a brief table relating to school lands funds setting forth the size of funds, expressed in thousands of dollars, the unsold lands, expressed in millions of acres, and the revenues from school lands and school lands funds expressed in thousands of dollars. I seek the unanimous consent of the committee to have this inserted in Hansard at this point.

The situation today is this. The revenues from school lands as a percentage of provincial expenditure on education declined in Manitoba from 9.5 per cent in 1945-46 to 3.5 per cent in 1957-58. In Saskatchewan, the revenues from school lands were 21.9 per cent of educational expenditures in 1945-46 and 14.2 per cent in 1958-59. In Alberta, the school lands revenues constituted 12.9 per cent of educational expenditures in 1945-46 and 8.8 per cent in 1958-59.
The provinces have also contended that the retention of federal control over the use of the school lands and school lands funds in the three prairie provinces infringes upon their autonomy and that the existence of this legislative control involves unnecessary administrative work and impairs the financial flexibility of the provinces concerned. In the belief that the arguments advanced by the provinces were reasonable and in the desire to co-operate with the prairie provinces in this matter, the Prime Minister at the dominion-provincial conference of February 1961, suggested that the governments of Canada, Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta should enter into an agreement to confer on those provinces complete authority over their school lands and their school lands funds. The provinces were agreeable to such an arrangement and agreements to this effect have been entered into by the governments concerned. The house will be asked by the bill to be founded upon this resolution to approve on behalf of Canada the agreements entered into with the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta. The agreements as I said will become effective when they have also been approved by the legislatures of the provinces concerned.

Mr. Chairman, as the parliamentary secretary has indicated we are discussing an amendment to section 7 of the basic agreement between the federal government and the three prairie provinces entered into in 1930, removing any suggestion that these funds are to be regarded as trust funds and specially segregated and under special

Western School Lands Administration
rules in so far as income therefrom is concerned in the hands of the provincial governments.
I do not think the amendment to the original agreement that will likely appear in the bill will prove to be nearly as controversial or delaying in debate as was the original amendment introduced by the Mackenzie King government in 1930.
At that time the opposition of the day suggested that, notwithstanding that the agreement seemed to eliminate a long standing controversy and sense of grievance that existed in the prairie provinces because they did not appear to be on a similar basis as were the other provinces of Canada with respect to their natural resources under section 109, I believe, of the original British North America Act of 1867, and quite apart from any infringement of autonomy with respect to school lands, there were none the less other infringements of autonomy unlike the conditions that applied with respect to the natural resources of the older provinces. It was suggested that the federal government retained certain rights with respect to lands in which it had made investments for national parks, including mineral rights with respect thereto. Certain suggestions were made to the effect that there were also some restrictions on the prairie provinces with respect to water development unlike the situation in the older provinces. There was also the suggestion that by the retention of some federal rights with respect to lands that had already been designated as Indian reserves, the amendment of 1930 was unsatisfactory.
I wonder whether, as a result of the recent negotiations with these provinces which result in the present amendments to the 1930 agreement, the prairie provinces have indicated that they seek changes in the areas I have outlined and in the area of control of national parks. Of course, if control were to be released they might also seek control with respect to expenditures in relation to those territories designated as parks. Perhaps this control would fall to the provinces ipso facto. I wonder whether a request was made for control of mineral rights in the parks and whether there were negotiations with respect to lands designated as Indian reserves. In any event, we on this side have no quarrel with the proposed bill. It will leave the provinces unfettered. I take it that at the moment the control is largely in the segregation of revenues from those sources and certain stipulations as to the form of investment of those revenues. We have no quarrel with that. The requirements of the long standing Dominion Lands Act will no longer prevail. I think the parliamentary secretary indicated that the
pertinent sections of the Dominion Lands Act which will no longer prevail are sections 34 to 40. As I read the agreement, which was tabled last Friday, I take it that it involves section 37.

Mr. Chairman, one can be in this house for a number of years and yet always learn something. This afternoon I listened with interest to the historical background of those school lands of the three prairie provinces concerned, of their administration, of the sales and of the amendments to the original legislation to date given by the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance.
We support this legislation. It seems to us that these agreements are the result of negotiation. They are a sensible arrangement; they are in accord with the spirit of the times and of the wishes of the provinces concerned.

I should like to know whether this transfer of school lands would be subject to the performance by the province of Manitoba of its obligations under the Manitoba Act of 1870 or under the British North America Act of 1871. Section 6 of the latter act says:
Except as provided by the third section of this act, it shall not be competent for the parliament of Canada to alter the provisions of the last mentioned act of the said parliament, in so far as it relates to the province of Manitoba, or of any other act hereafter establishing new provinces in the said dominion, (e) subject always to the right of a legislature of the province of Manitoba to alter from time to time the provisions of any law respecting the qualification of electors and members of the legislative assembly, and to make laws respecting elections in the said province.
This shows that under the British North America Act of 1871 the province of Manitoba has no right to deal with school matters in that province in connection with the rights reserved by the act except subject to what is mentioned in the section I have just read. I take it that if there is any transfer of school lands to the province of Manitoba it should be made clear and understood that they are transferred subject to the performance by the province of its obligations under the British North America Act and the Manitoba Act of 1870.
