(Translation):

subtopic: CONSTRUCTION OF LINE TO GREAT SLAVE LAKE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I understand that the government has amended Part I of Bill C-71 as proposed so that it may seem a little more attractive to civil servants.
Subsection (1) of section 7 reads as follows:
The Minister of Finance or such members of the public service as he may designate shall from time to time consult with representatives of appropriate organizations and associations of employees-
It is further stated in subsection 2:
The commission and such members of the public service as the Minister of Finance may designate shall from time to time consult with representatives of appropriate organizations and associations of employees-
Then, in subsection 3:
The commission and such members of the public with representatives of appropriate organizations and associations of employees-
I quite agree that it is an improvement over the first bill. On the other hand, that is exactly the opposite of what the civil servants' associations have been asking for. They asked for the right to bargain at any time and not only when the minister would deem it proper to call them in. All the associations agreed on that point; they asked for the right to bargain directly. They insisted on the right for civil servants to open negotiations with any representative of the government whom the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) may care to designate. We raised that point in the committee but that did not seem to please the government's representatives.
It was claimed that this would perhaps deprive parliament of the right to settle problems. In my opinion, the prerogatives of parliament are not involved because even if civil servants were given bargaining rights or arbitration, the funds to pay their salaries would still have to be voted by parliament and if the latter did not approve them, there would be no question of salary increases.
It was also submitted that such a thing could lead to claims for the right to strike on the part of civil servants. Well, we know that, before the committee, representatives from the different civil servant associations clearly indicated that they were opposed to the right to strike, except the Canadian postal employees association which requested that right.

As a matter of fact, I wonder why it is said that there is danger that some day the civil servants will decide to strike, because neither in the existing legislation nor in the former act, chapter 48 in the revised statutes, nor in the present amendments, do I see anything forbidding them to strike now. Well, when something is not forbidden, it follows that it is allowed, but the civil servants have no intention of taking advantage of this situation to go on strike.
Moreover, we know that in Saskatchewan, government employees have the right to bargain, to negotiate directly with the government, and it has been like that for some time now. However, the employees have not made use of the right to put the government in a difficult situation. They simply benefit-ted by that and the government did not complain. Besides, in most provinces there are some means of forcing the government to negotiate with civil servants and even in the province of Quebec, where there is no special formula, section 5 of the civil service act provides that, when the commission is made up of three members, one of them shall be appointed upon the recommendation of the general council of employees. In this way, the employees have at least a representative on the commission to protect their interests.
Furthermore, in Ontario, under the law, a four member advisory committee has been set up; three of its members are appointed by the lieutenant governor in council according to set rules, and the fourth upon a recommendation made under the provisions of the civil service act. The rules enacted under the civil service act, also provide for the creation of a public service grievance board composed of at least three members appointed by the lieutenant governor in council.
Civil servants' associations may represent an employee who wishes to submit his grievances. Again, this is bound to improve the situation, and much better than what is now provided in the bill, because it now says: "the minister must consult, from time to time"; the minister must consult but when are employees entitled to demand consultations from the department? Never, since the minister alone can decide when civil servants may come and discuss contentious issues. But civil servants may never, according to the bill, even as amended, require that the government undertake discussions with employees of the commission and civil service associations.
In section 45 of Manitoba's civil service act, the maintenance of a joint council is provided. The provincial secretary and two

members of the cabinet represent the government; therefore, three ministers represent the government. The association appoints three members who are supposed to represent the civil servants. And, further on, it is noted that a member of the civil service commission and the executive secretary of the association may attend a meeting of the joint council and of the government in an advisory capacity. It is a great improvement on what we have, and on what the Ottawa government is now proposing.

(Translation):
In Saskatchewan, negotiations are carried out with a staff association certified as a negotiating agent, which has union status under the union act. Those negotiations are conducted on questions of salaries and other working conditions attached to positions in the classified service. Salaries for those positions excluded from the collective agreement, are established by a committee on salaries which reviews representations made by the
Civil Service Act
department involved. There is a right to appeal after rates of salary have been established.
This is similar with what we are asking for. It is similar to what staff associations in our civil service are asking for. It involves the right to initiate negotiations with the government even though the minister is not willing to go into negotiations. And when negotiations are carried out between representatives of the department, selected by the department, and representatives of the variousxStaff associations in the civil service, if they do not come to an agreement, we want some kind of an arbitration board to examine their grievances. And I take as a grievance at the present time, the fact of ascertaining whether the employees are right or wrong in demanding a reasonable salary or normal working conditions.
In Alberta, since 1923, the public service act provides for a joint council composed of three members appointed by the association and three members selected by the provincial government. Such council is the negotiating body on salaries, working conditions and grievances. The provincial secretary treasurer acts as chairman of the joint council. He is the counterpart of the Minister of Finance.
Generally speaking, agreement is achieved first at the level of the joint council whose recommendations are almost always accepted.
In British Columbia, under section 72 of the civil service act of that province, the government has to recognize a civil service association which represents more than half of all the public employees whenever questions relating to the welfare of the civil employees and their working conditions, including their salaries, are raised.
That provision does not exclude the right of appeal or discussion with one particular civil servant or a minority group among the staff.
This is the kind of association, the kind of union that is needed to satisfy the justified complaints of civil service associations, because until now they have been treated rather like second class citizens.
People say: "But how can they make such demands"?
I recall that before 1890, when workers in industry or other employees made such demands, i.e. the right to negotiate directly with their employers-they were considered as revolutionaries, or even communists and jailed. I know many labour leaders who had

Civil Service Act
to spend several weeks in jail because they had simply demanded what we are claiming now for civil servants.
But today, try and say in the labour world or elsewhere and say that the one who is claiming direct bargaining rights is revolutionary minded or a communist. No one will believe you because every human being has the right of discussion with his employer. It is a bounden right and you cannot take him to task or refuse him that right. Whether he is a factory worker or a government employee, he has that same right to try and protect through the power of an association his natural rights, and to protect himself against anyone who infringes his rights.
That is what the civil servants, members of every association, have come to ask for. They insisted. But the government does not seem prepared to grant their request. However, it is very simple, for our amendment reads as follows:
7 (1) The commission, and such members of the public service as the Minister of Finance may designate, shall negotiate directly with representatives of appropriate organizations and associations of employees of the crown, with respect to pay and other terms and conditions of employment, at the request of such representatives, or wherever in the opinion of the commission or the Minister of Finance, as the case may be, such negotiation and consultation is necessary or desirable in the interests of the civil service or the government. Such direct negotiation and consultation shall be initiated by either the governor in council, its appointees, or the appropriate staff associations and organizations noted above.
(2)	Where negotiation does not result in agreement, the matter under dispute shall be taken to an arbitration tribunal by either party.
(3)	The results of such negotiation and/or arbitration shall be proclaimed by a suitable instrument, where necessary subject to the approval of parliament.
Now, there is a reservation made that parliament approval is needed on all those matters of arbitration or bargaining, which means that parliament is not ignored and that its prerogatives are respected.
So, I hope the government will reconsider and understand that civil servants must be treated on the same basis as employees in all other parts of Canada and indeed the whole world. Public servants must be regarded as first class citizens like all other citizens of this country; that is all we are asking in the amendment we moved when we considered this bill at the end of June or early in July.
So, I hope the government will reconsider its stand and accept the proposed amendment in order that federal civil servants be considered as first class employees.

Dag Hammarskjold died tragically and prematurely but, as I believe he would have wished, in the service of peace and the United Nations. He was indefatigable; he was wise; and he was entirely selfless in his devotion to his work. He was as sure and as resolute in carrying out instructions from the United Nations for international action in the cause of peace as he was skilful and objective in seeking to establish a basis for that action in the charter. As well as being an extremely dedicated servant of peace and the international community he was a most brilliant and cultivated gentleman and a good and loyal friend.
The world can ill afford to lose such a great man, especially at this time. His life was a triumph of service and achievement, and his passing at the very height of his powers is a tragic loss. His death should inspire all of us to do what we can to secure the triumph of the cause for which he died, peace and security in the world through the United Nations.

speechtext:
that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure respecting the observance of the centennial of confederation in Canada and in relation thereto,-
1.	To provide for the constitution of a corporation called the national centennial administration;
2.	To provide for the establishment of a national conference on Canada's centennial;
3.	To provide for the objects, purposes and powers of the administration and of the conference; and

Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Chown in the chair.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR NATIONAL CORPORATION, NATIONAL CONFERENCE, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think it is only proper that I should make a rather complete statement respecting this matter at this time. The resolution is a prelude to a bill to establish the machinery for undertaking the dominion government's part in the observance of Canada's centennial. Although the centennial itself is nearly six years away, much preliminary work has already been done.
I think it will be agreed that the centennial is more than a holiday or an occasion for festive celebrations. I was reading yesterday some of the debates at the time of confederation and immediately thereafter. In reference to the celebrations, Sir John Macdonald said that a great opportunity was lost in 1867 when the dominion was formed out of the several provinces. This remarkable event in the history of the British empire passed almost without notice.
All during the years there have been references made to the fact that, for some reason or other, there were no celebrations other than desultory ones restricted to a few areas within the confederating provinces of that day. On this occasion, however, we will be celebrating the hundredth anniversary of our country. It should be a time of national stocktaking and of rededication to the future.
90205-6-534
Canadian Centennial
It will represent a dramatic year in Canadian history and an opportunity for Canadians to develop a fuller understanding of what it means and can mean to be a Canadian. One of the aims of the centennial observance should be to make Canadians aware of their unique heritage and their birth right, and of the contributions to our development that have been made by the peoples of the founding races as well as the many other nationalities who have come to our country.
I think it is not generally known that Canada played a very large part in the history of religious freedom. Indeed, the United Kingdom parliament in 1775 granted religious freedom to what is now Canada long in advance of it being granted in the United Kingdom. Further in that connection, I might mention that it was in Canada, some 25 years in advance of the same rights being attained in the United Kingdom, that those of the Jewish race received equality and the privilege of electing members of that faith to the House of Commons.
It is of interest to think of the beginnings of confederation, the arguments that were advanced by Sir John Macdonald and those associated with him, and the stand taken by those opposed to confederation. Following this there were meetings in Quebec and in Charlottetown. I was in the archives the other day and I found there a most interesting document. This is a report of the resolutions adopted at the conference of delegates from the provinces of Canada. I have a photographic summary of it, and it sets fortl; the basis of the proposed confederation of the provinces and colonies at a conference held in the city of Quebec in October, 1864. It sets out in detail the changes that were made. This is Macdonald's copy and it is covered with doodling, apparently drawings by Sir John of the various representatives at that conference, indicating a higher degree of art than has been displayed by any of his successors. I cannot place it on Hansard but I can say this, that there were few persons who were not honoured by having their features drawn.
The document sets out the views of that meeting and the various changes which were made, and which brought about a federation that few believed would have been possible. As may be seen through a reading of the document and also through a reading of the debates between 1860 and 1867, as was stated by Sir Wilfrid Laurier at the time of Sir John A. Macdonald's death, the vision of Sir John A. Macdonald and his associates was underlined and emphasized. Indeed, it was the work of Sir John Macdonald and Sir George Etienne Cartier that made possible the

Canadian Centennial
transformation of colonial North America into the self governing country into which it has grown. Had it not been for their work there would never have been possible the development of the commonwealth concept of today.
There were few in the United Kingdom who believed that it would be possible to bring about confederation. It was Lafon-taine who would not accept the views of Lord John Russell and other imperial leaders that self government being granted to the colonies would mean the breaking up of the ties with the United Kingdom. It was Lafon-taine who foresaw that if representative self government was granted, the relations between the United Kingdom and the self governing possessions beyond the seas would be strengthened, not weakened. Macdonald and Cartier refused to accept the view of John Stuart Mill that parliamentary institutions could not live in a country that had two or more ethnic stocks.
Of all the countries of the commonwealth today-and this is something we sometimes forget-Canada was the first to attain responsible, representative and parliamentary government and the first, as I said a moment ago, to develop the federal system which in its essence made possible the uniting of areas representing various races, geographic separations and the like. It is a system that is being followed more and more in various parts of the developing commonwealth, and has been the contribution which has made possible the West Indies Federation and which within the next couple of years will make possible the Malayan confederation provided agreement is arrived at among Malaya, Singapore, Borneo, Sarawak and Brunei. These are some of the matters which are of the past which recall some things that are often forgotten.
It was on February 19, 1865 that the "Attorney General West," Sir John A. Macdonald, introduced the resolution which read as follows:
That an humble address be presented to Her Majesty, praying that she may be graciously pleased to cause a measure to be submitted to the imperial parliament for the purpose of uniting the colonies of Canada, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Newfoundland and Prince Edward Island into one government with provisions based on certain resolutions, which were adopted at a conference of delegates from the said colonies held at the city of Quebec, on the 10th October 1864.
Speaking to the measure on February 6, 1865, Sir John said this:
When this union takes place, we will be at the outset no inconsiderable people. We find ourselves with a population approaching four millions of souls. Such a population in Europe would make a second, or at least, a third rate power. And with a rapidly increasing population-for X am satisfied that under this union our population will increase in a still greater ratio than ever before-with

increased credit-with a higher position in the eyes of Europe-with the increased security we can offer to immigrants, who would naturally prefer to seek a new home in what is known to them as a great country, than in any one little colony or another-with all this I am satisfied that, great as has been our increase in the last twenty five years since the union between Upper and Lower Canada, our future progress, during the next quarter of a century, will be vastly greater. And when, by means of this rapid increase, we become a nation of eight or nine millions of inhabitants, our alliance will be worthy of being sought by the great nations of the earth.
He pictured the day ahead when there would be greatness on the part of Canada that would assure its recognition by the great countries of the world. So it was with Cartier, McGee and many others who spoke at that time. So we will celebrate an event great in its past and, I believe, greater in its future.
The systematic preparation of plans for the centennial, as I said, is already under way. It began two years ago. In February, 1960 the national committee on the centennial was inaugurated. This committee provides a means of consultation between the federal government and the governments of the provinces in matters relating to the centennial. The federal government is represented on the committee by the Minister of Transport and the Minister of Fisheries, who are joint chairmen, the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration and the Minister of Agriculture. Each of the provinces is represented by a minister and one other representative. The national committee has shown a high degree of unanimity on the significance of the centennial and on the general objectives to be sought. At its inaugural meeting the national committee set up four working committees to study the historical, cultural, ceremonial and administrative aspects of the planning.
Canadians everywhere were invited some 16 months ago to send in their suggestions as to how Canada's centennial might best be observed. This invitation provoked a healthy response. Indeed, if the projects that were suggested were adopted it would involve the expenditure of several billions of dollars. I have a list of the suggestions that were made. I think it might be well for me to table it, if the committee will agree, as they are indicative of the comprehensive nature of the representations and may be provocative of other suggestions from those who have given and are giving thought to this matter.
The suggestions range from proposals for pageants of different kinds to the building of a special centennial city; from postage stamp and coin issues to festivals of the arts; and from the eradication of particular diseases to the publication of biographies. It has also been suggested that special recognition should be given to the need for the

commemoration of the 1864 conferences in Charlottetown and Quebec which were the precursors of confederation.
I think I should pause for a moment to refer to the work being done by the committee or organization set up for the building of a confederation commemorative building in the city of Charlottetown. The committee is representative of all parts of the country and already has done much toward bringing about the building in question and also festivities to celebrate the conference that took place in that city.
The planning problem is, therefore, not to devise suitable projects but to select the most suitable ones. The federal-provincial working committees have been studying and assessing the various suggestions. The next meeting will take place in Ottawa on October 11.
The federal government has given consideration to the kinds of projects it should undertake. It is particularly impressed by the fact that the centennial will provide the opportunity for the execution of projects of a lasting nature. Last month the Minister of Public Works announced the first major centennial project, when he made it known that the government had decided to authorize the national capital commission to purchase land and buildings on Sussex drive, Ottawa. The project will be a rare opportunity for the preservation of those things that go back to confederation, and will make possible what has been described as "a mile of living history".
A number of non-government organizations have also begun preparations. In May, 1960 the Canadian centenary council was formed by these organizations. Its membership now comprises 125 national organizations and its purposes are to stimulate public interest in the centennial observances and to provide information and planning service to national organizations in this regard.
I realize that I cannot refer in any particular to the bill that will be introduced following the acceptance by the committee of this resolution. However, I would point out that it will have two principal divisions. The first will be the establishment of a national centennial administration which will assume responsibility for the planning and execution of programs of the federal government relating to the centennial. The national centennial administration will consist of a commissioner, a deputy commissioner and not more than eight directors, and to avoid duplication of functions it will work wherever possible through existing departments and agencies of the federal government.
Then, too, a second major provision will be the establishment of a national conference on
90205-6-5341
Canadian Centennial
the centennial. This will not be an administrative body but will be a forum where the centennial can be viewed and discussed as a whole by governmental and non-governmental representatives. Centennial activities will inevitably involve many elements and have various sponsors. Therefore special efforts will be required to give these activities some measure of unity and to guard against a formless jumble of individual projects. This conference will consist of a chairman who will be either the Prime Minister or such other minister as will be designated by the governor in council, and not more than 60 members appointed by the governor in council. Of these, two members will represent each of the provinces and will be appointed on the recommendation of the government of each of the provinces. The other representatives will be chosen from every major segment of Canadian life.
I feel the committee will agree that the observance of the centennial should reflect the whole range of Canada's history and not merely confederation itself. The program should not be designed merely to commemorate a past event, but to stir the imagination of the Canadian people and give to the people as a whole a sense of national progress and national unity. The centennial should be one in which every citizen will have an opportunity to play his or her part. I think the two bodies to be established will help to ensure that the aims and purposes of this one hundredth anniversary can be fully realized thereby. Although Ottawa will be the administrative and focal point, every region of Canada should avail itself of this great occasion.
It will be the role of the federal government, not to erect a giant superstructure but merely to assist and co-ordinate. The true expression of pride and fulfilment will, I hope, come largely from local levels. In each and every community in this country there is a wealth of local flavour and difference which should be emphasized in the national interest. Wherever possible or feasible the bigger national attractions should, I feel, be made portable so that all the provinces of Canada can share in the nation's birthday. I believe that nothing would be more beneficial than for a national train to be set up and travel fi om one end of Canada to the other, carrying thereon the documents of Canada's historical background, the constitutional documents, as well as those charters of freedom that are ours by reason of our heritage.
As Canada is a country on the threshold of an exciting tomorrow, the centennial should serve as a launching pad for new triumphs in her second century. We should

Canadian Centennial
honour history. At the same time a true birthday party should span the three dimensions of time, a national salute in retrospect, an appraisal of the present and a toast to the century to come.
Our history has been inextricably woven into the struggle against geography and climate. Courage in the face of formidable odds is the theme which I believe should run through the celebration that will take place, for this country is a land in which the odysseys of the explorers, the missionaries and the leaders of the past should be made available to all Canadians. As I read yesterday something of the events at the time of confederation and prior thereto it gave me a pride that can only come from a knowledge of what has been wrought by the hand of history. During the year to come I believe we should try to renew our past so that it becomes part of the possession of all Canadians, and at the same time lay the foundations for a greater future.
We are a creditor nation with historic ties to Great Britain and France. We are a creditor nation to most of the nations of men. We should emphasize the international aspect of being Canadian. If we do that, I feel our centennial celebrations will be a magnet to draw visitors from all around the earth. This will be Canada's year to appraise, admire and adjust. It will require a great deal of work and preparation. It will require not imitation but inspiration and imagination to properly reveal the Canada that is ours. I recall the words of Daniel Burnham who, when commenting on the plans for building the capital city of Washington in the United States, said this:
Make no little plans. They have no magic to stir men's blood, and probably themselves will not be realized. Make big plans, aim high in hope and work, remembering that a noble and logical diagram once recorded will never die but long alter we are gone will be a living thing, asserting itself with ever growing insistency. Remember that our sons and grandsons are going to do things that would stagger us. Let your watchword be order and your beacon beauty.
I hope that all governments, federal, provincial and local, will be inspired by this one hundredth anniversary of our country to build for tomorrow, to fuse the functional with the beautiful, the concordant with the useful. The shaping of national destiny is no different from individual destiny, because we are the moulders of the future of our country. Fate itself plays a part, but more so does the work of those who contribute to the building of the kind of country that all of us hope will be wrought.
On January 18, 1904, Sir Wilfrid Laurier replied to the toast to Canada, and in that speech he stated what the hope of the future would be; that the twentieth century would
[Mr. Diefenbaker.l
be Canada's. That is what this festival will emphasize, a stirring occasion so that Canadians may hold the nation's sights high upon the horizon.
I trust the committee will give unanimous support to this resolution and that in a spirit of unity all of us, whether in the federal parliament, in provincial legislatures or in the municipalities will join together and bring about an imaginative program so that we may relive our past and rededicate this land to its future, the hopes for which were spoken of so eloquently by those who were present at the birth of its institutions.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR NATIONAL CORPORATION, NATIONAL CONFERENCE, ETC.
speechtext:
I think all members of this committee wherever they may sit would wish to give wholehearted support to this resolution. It is perhaps a happy coincidence that the Prime Minister on his sixty sixth birthday anniversary should be reminding us that our nation will soon be celebrating its one hundredth birthday anniversary. It is appropriate that we should prepare for that celebration.
A centenary is, of course, a momentous occasion in the history of a state. During the years since 1867 we have seen the completion of the geographical boundaries of confederation with the happy and fortunate union only a few years ago of Newfoundland with the rest of our homeland. We have, then, completed our boundaries nationally in that sense. But Canada is a new and developing country, and there is still much to be done. There are new horizons to be enlarged; there are frontiers to be pushed back and there are regions to be developed. In that sense we Canadians still have the excitements and the incentives which are usually attached to a new and developing society. While this is true, the fact that we shall soon be celebrating our hundredth birthday makes us one of the older states in the world.
As the Prime Minister has said, this celebration should encompass the whole range of Canada's history, not merely the achievement of confederation itself. The right hon. gentleman indicated how this could be done. It should certainly be celebrated in a way which is worthy of the occasion, not merely by ceremonies and memorials, which may be exciting but which will be ephemeral, but also in a more permanent way.
It is interesting in this regard to examine the various proposals which have been made for this purpose, and there are a great many of them. The Prime Minister made reference to this. I have before me the first report of the Canadian centennial council. If all these suggestions-and they are very interesting ones indeed-were carried out we should

need the whole centennial year in which to implement them. One of the subcommittees of the committee has suggested-and I think it is a wise suggestion and one we should be thinking about even now-that no celebration of our centenary would be complete unless by 1967 we had taken all the necessary legislative actions-and these things, I know, are not easy to do-which would complete, in the words of the recommendation, "our full autonomy as a nation".
The centenary council has also made suggestions which as I have indicated should be of value in establishing a permanent recognition of our centenary, by action which will not be temporary but which will redound over the years ahead to the benefit of all Canadians. In this regard they have put forward some very imaginative proposals. One suggestion is a program to remove from our country underdeveloped or depressed communities; also to ensure that in the future no Canadian in this country will be denied access to higher education because of a lack of funds. Perhaps along these lines we will be able to recognize in an enduring and valuable way some of the benefits we as Canadians have been fortunate enough to receive during our first hundred years. This recognition should be deepened and extended. We should take action in this centenary celebration to emphasize our national dignity and national destiny, to make life better for all of our people.
Also, as the Prime Minister has pointed out, it would be appropriate to re-examine the values of our national society, and to resolve that we will do perhaps more than we have been able to do in the past to strengthen those values, based as they are on the enduring concept of freedom, and based as they are also in a political sense on the foundation of the two cultures, two languages and two traditions of the two founding peoples. Some years before confederation, when Lord Durham came to Canada, hon. members will recall that he said he found in Canada-and I think I am quoting his words correctly-two nations warring in the bosom of a single state. In the years that have passed since that statement was made there has been a change from conflict to co-operation. While in the cultural sense, in the racial sense, in the linguistic sense and indeed in the sense of separate traditions while we have-in that sense-two nations, nevertheless we now have two nations, co-operating in the bosom of a single state.
These two races, two cultures, and two nations in that sense, as the Prime Minister has pointed out, have been enriched in the
Canadian Centennial
years that have followed by people of practically every strain, race and culture from all parts of the world. To use the Prime Minister's own phrase we are indeed a creditor nation in that way, as well as a creditor nation in the sense that we have a dual foundation of the two basic races.
As has been pointed out, not very much attention was given to Canada's future, her destiny and potential greatness at the time of confederation. But the men in those days built better than perhaps even they knew. People in the mother countries did not realize then that in North America a strong new state had arisen dedicated to freedom, to human welfare and to the things that make life worth living for man when he bands himself together in a political society. As we approach our centennial year I think we can be proud of our growth, our progress and our achievements, but we can be proud without being smug. We can demonstrate that pride in the way we celebrate our centenary. One means which occurs to me, and there are many, to show our pride in our nation is by making our capital worthy in every way of its position as the heart and core of that nation.
The Prime Minister has outlined some of the organizations which will be set up, and it is appropriate that they should be set up at this time to make this occasion worthy of its historic import. He indicated that there will be a combination of public and private planning in that regard and that, of course, is the way it should be done. We on this side will be glad to support the steps which the government is proposing to this end.
Our nation has a great destiny ahead of it if we wish to make it so, and if man's inhumanity to man makes it possible for any nation to have a good destiny. It is appropriate, then, that as we discuss this resolution we should remind ourselves of our past and look forward with confidence to the future of what Charles Dickens so many years ago called this happy, hopeful land.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR NATIONAL CORPORATION, NATIONAL CONFERENCE, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, on behalf of this group I rise to express our wholehearted and complete support for the spirit and purpose of this resolution, which reflects the wishes of the vast majority of Canadians at this time. Throughout the years there have been numerous references to the centennial celebration. I think it is correct to say that the first time it was brought to the attention of any large group was at the Ontario provincial convention of the C.C.F. in 1950. It was raised on that occasion and discussed.
Later on the then hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre placed on the order paper

Canadian Centennial
a resolution dealing with this subject. It was first introduced, I believe, in 1954 and was reintroduced in 1955, 1956 and 1957. In that latter year there occurred the first debate on that resolution, which I shall now place on the record because it was considered very comprehensive:

speakeroldname: Mr. Stanley Knowles (Winnipeg North Centre) moved:
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR NATIONAL CORPORATION, NATIONAL CONFERENCE, ETC.
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should give consideration to the advisability of the establishment of a 100th anniversary committee, with provision for federal and provincial representation, for the purpose of planning the economic and social development of this country on a vast scale, including inter alia housing and slum clearance, conservation, irrigation and power projects, improvements in transportation, highway construction, the elimination of grade crossings, the building of hospitals, assistance to municipal projects and other public works, and also for the purpose of planning ways and means to strengthen the economy of every section of this country; and that consideration should be given to the advisability of such a program being launched immediately and being pursued vigorously year by year so that on July 1, 1967, the people of Canada will be in a position to celebrate this nation's 100th birthday not only with fireworks and speeches but by the achievement of a land of health and abundance for all our people.
During the debate the hon. gentleman received support in principle from all hon. members who participated in the discussion. There was some criticism of the rather comprehensive nature of this resolution. I had the opportunity of participating in the debate. As we saw it at that time this was a resolution to focus attention upon desirable objectives to strive toward and accomplish by 1967. The hon. gentleman moved this resolution and spoke to it at some length, believing it would focus attention on this subject so that our celebration in 1967 would not only be a celebration in the ordinary sense of the word, a happy time, but in the deeper sense of having reality and meaning.
In listening to the Prime Minister I was very interested in his historical review of past developments and in certain statements he made respecting the approach and attitude of prominent people in Canadian history. I am one who always enjoys reading history. I find that history of the past is an antidote to the irritations of the present. I was interested also in his explanation of the proposed procedures which provide for federal and provincial co-operation and also cooperation with local communities. I am one who believes, as I am sure all members of this group firmly believe, that for an event of this type to be a success you must have co-operation among all communities in Canada; that success is dependent upon co-operation from the local level up no matter how small the community.

I cannot help but recall that I spent the fiftieth anniversary of confederation in a military hospital. You know, Mr. Chairman, some people have suggested that I might celebrate the one hundredth anniversary as a member of the government, but I might explain they have been very few in number to date. However, with a common pride in our history, in our achievements, in our hopes and in our aspirations, we can all look forward to this centennial as an opportunity to recognize the work of the pioneers and people of the past, to express our thanks for what they have done to provide the circumstances under which we live.
I often think there is insufficient understanding of the labours of people of the past in all groups of society who have given us so many of the things we enjoy today, the freedoms, the privileges and the material things of life. We can give thanks and celebrate in the knowledge that all Canadians are proud of the fact that by that time we shall have evolved national and provincial policies that will make certain that we are going to conserve and develop our natural resources, having in mind the welfare of the generations to come; because regardless of legislation, parties and theories, unless we conserve our natural resources we shall have nothing to build on in the future and no wealth to distribute.
In addition, Mr. Chairman, I trust that by 1967 we shall be able to celebrate the fact that every child in Canada will have the opportunity to obtain all the education he is capable of taking advantage of; that every person in Canada willing and able to work will have employment; that all Canadians will be provided with satisfactory health services; that all the disabled and those ill in Canada, suffering from disabilities of various kinds, from whatever source they may arise, will be provided with a measure of comfort and security at the expense of us all, and that our senior citizens will continue to live in security with a measure of comfort. We believe these are objectives that we should work toward so that we can celebrate in 1967 with the knowledge that these are accomplishments.
The members of this group are glad to cooperate with all who are working to that end. We believe that with purpose, with determination, with energy and imagination we can succeed in reaching those objectives by 1967. To those objectives we must all march if we are going to succeed, and those objectives must be reached, in our opinion, if we are to celebrate our one hundredth anniversary in every sense of the word as an event that Canadians are proud of.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, on behalf of my French speaking fellow citizens, I should like to express, in my mother tongue, what we feel at the announcement of the celebrations which will, in a few years from now, mark the centenary of the Canadian constitution.
These celebrations will take on a distinctive character for all Canadians, more particularly because we realize that it is thanks to the pact of confederation that we developed as a nation and that we succeeded in burying the quarrels which, unfortunately, in 1867 threatened to plunge this nation into civil war.
When we consider the great country Canada is today, we cannot but think of the tremendous sacrifices made by our forefathers to found this country which now holds such an important place in the world.
When we consider the tremendous efforts which those pioneers from European countries had to make and the severity of the weather they had to endure in clearing this foreign land to set up their homes, we are filled with wonder and admiration. Indeed, those men deserve the tribute we want to pay them in the coming celebrations. And we want to pay a particular tribute to those men of genius who established this confederation pact which is the very basis, the strength of the nation.
We salute those men of character, Lafon-taine and Baldwin, who were able to establish the rule of justice in the houses of parliament.
We salute the genius of Macdonald and Cartier to whom we owe this confederation which is the cornerstone of the greatness of Canada.
It is actually due to confederation that peace has existed in this country since 1867. It is because of this pact that the respective rights and privileges of both great races which form our nation have been respected.
It is also through the confederative pact that the bi-ethnic and bi-cultural character of the nation has been preserved.
Finally, thanks to this agreement this country has achieved a national unity which is strengthening and enables us to live today not in a divided Canada but in a united Canada, a large and a strong Canada, where the future can be faced with confidence.
Since 1867, long strides have been made in every field of endeavour.
Canadian industry has reached gigantic proportions, trade is in the process of considerably expanding and increasing from day to day, and in the intellectual field we
Canadian Centennial
now have distinctive Canadian culture and art and a definite Canadian way of thinking. So it can be stated that since confederation gigantic steps have been accomplished towards the achievement and development of national life and thought. This is only a beginning.
Today the whole world's attention is focused on our country; other nations realize that we have in Canada, a tremendous potential and that there is a future for all who wish to settle here and associate themselves with those who have done so much already so that Canada could become what it is today. Canadians have achieved all these things because the highest principles of human ideals were guiding them. Canadians believe in freedom and every time the freedom of humankind was threatened, Canadians were among the first who wanted to protect that ideal against the barbarian onslaught threatening civilization.
During those two great wars, our soldiers fought with unrivalled courage. They fought on the battlefields of Europe and other continents not only to protect themselves but also in order that the ideals of kindness and justice they believed in could survive in this world. Those soldiers were the defenders of right, justice and truth.
We bow to those who have laid down their lives for those principles, to those who suffered on the battlefields and who, still bear today the scars of their glorious wounds. Moreover, we bow to the courage of all these men who, without exception, were the ambassadors of Canadian feeling, by defending in foreign lands the most beautiful and greatest thing of all: human freedom.
Our country, Mr. Chairman, is in full bloom, and the eyes of all men are turned in this direction. One only has to go abroad to realize that other countries sometimes view with envy what is being done in Canada. However, it is very easy to notice admiration everywhere for our accomplishments.
I believe it is our duty to thank Providence for having given so much to us Canadians. In fact, poverty is the lot of many countries which have been torn by terrible strife and which, even today, are threatened by revolutions.
I believe that it is necessary to repeat, whenever possible, Mr. Chairman, that there exists, here, in Canada, beauty, greatness, order, wealth, and belief in those principles of life: freedom and respect for human rights.

Canadian Centennial
I believe that it is absolutely essential to prepare with care the celebration of our centennial, to prepare it in such a way that it will attract millions of tourists who will be able to see for themselves the excellence of our democratic way of life. Those tourists may return home with a strong desire to imitate what is being done in our country, and they may even know the happiness which is ours.
If there is one reproach that could be made to the Canadian people, it is that they do not fully realize how lucky they are, and that they fail to appreciate their blessings in their own country. We too often hear politicians and others criticize everything that happens here, exaggerate certain social or economic problems that are serious, I agree, but that are, after all, not as serious as some events happening in other countries where the danger of revolution and communism is always present. Instead of readily criticizing what is happening in our country, instead of taking pleasure in blaming our leaders constantly, regardless of their political affiliation and of the field of their activities, it seems to me it would be better for every Canadian citizen to help with his advice those who are called upon to administer the country. In my opinion, they will always be glad to accept advice from right-minded people who have public interest at heart.
Mr. Chairman, I feel that it is essential to act in that way because prophets of doom and gloom will be pleased to sow doubt and anxiety in the minds of men, thus making it possible for communism, that horrible ideology which dominates so many countries, to get a foothold in Canada.
I hope that all French Canadian organizations, without exception, will join in the preparations for the centennial. Whether on the cultural, intellectual and social levels or in the industrial field, all Canadians who love their country must take an interest in this historic event.
Our country is in full progress and development. By taking an active part in the preparations for the centennial celebrations, the citizens will, in the years to come, work efficiently for Canada. I know that all French Canadians love Canada like I do. Perhaps some people love our country as much as I do, but certainly no one loves it more. I invite them to join with us who are entrusted with public affairs and who are anxious to

make of the centennial celebrations of our confederation, the greatest event in our history.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR NATIONAL CORPORATION, NATIONAL CONFERENCE, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I wish to join with the Associate Minister of National Defence (Mr. Sevigny) and say that we agree that the statesmen of 1867 and previous years had to make great sacrifices in order to implement confederation. All the politicians put aside party feelings to bring forth the fullest national unity possible and thus bring into being an institution that neither the years nor difficulties could overcome.
Since then, as the Associate Minister of National Defence has said, we have been enjoying domestic peace, and we wonder whether such a thing would have been possible without confederation, because at that moment there was no friendship to spare between the Quebec Catholic group and the Ontario Anglo-Protestant group, and it was feared that one or the other would try to gain domination of the country by force.
But when the fathers of confederation paved the way to a federation of the existing provinces and of other provinces which could be formed later on, they found the right formula for two different races to live together and to co-operate for the good of Canada.
The rights and privileges of both races have been respected and I can say that almost every leader of the country has since recognized the necessity of maintaining that duality which is beneficial and profitable to the country. I hope that it will be maintained.
I readily recognize that here and there people have been found who did not understand the objectives of the fathers of confederation; that was to be expected because there will always be groups not sufficiently mature to realize what a great achievement it was and how essential has been the participation of two races and two ethnic groups.
It is agreed that since confederation, Canada has made gigantic progress. The small colony of that time has grown into an independent country and a member of the British commonwealth, as well as a nation in control of its own destiny. Canada has made tremendous progress in the fields of trade and industry and is well known the world over for her contribution to the welfare of the peoples of the world. In the field of diplomacy, we have had Canadians who have acquired wide recognition and who will continue to stand out.

In the fields of arts and culture, there has been remarkable improvement. True, we have not yet reached the quality of the masterpieces found in European countries because we lack the atmosphere conducive to the production of truly Canadian works. As far as literature is concerned, we have finally gone ahead in recent years and developed a truly Canadian literature. And with the help of the Canada Council and the continuing assistance of the various governments in office, we shall soon see the arts and literature flourish in Canada, as they should.
As the Associate Minister of National Defence said, Canada, twice at least, came to the rescue of European nations that needed support to preserve their freedoms and welfare. It did so with pleasure, and the sacrifices made have been recognized.
However, I would suggest to the Prime Minister that the time has come perhaps, since we are to celebrate the centenary of confederation, when Canada might give its armies, spread out across the world, a really distinctive, personal and specific flag, showing no sign whatever of interdependence, in order to prove that Canada has reached its maturity. I think such a project would be accepted by the great majority of the Canadian people, and even if some did object to that, they would be in a small minority that would eventually bow before the majority, as it has always happened since 1867.

speechtext: Very well.

I should now like to close my remarks with these few words taken from a Canadian song:
Foreigners see with an envious eye the majestic flow of the St. Lawrence.
Well, foreigners not only see the St. Lawrence with an envious eye, they also see our way of life, our working methods and our democratic spirit. In fact I do not think there is a country in the world where democracy is better understood than in Canada.
I hope we shall be able to celebrate in a grand and glorious way the centenary of confederation, and that our successors will be able to say that Canada is constantly making gigantic steps forward.

This measure is obviously one that will receive the support of all parties in this house. It therefore needs little debate. No matter where we sit, I think we are all aware of and appreciate the sense 90205-6-535

of history of our Prime Minister. We hope this measure will receive his constant personal interest. In our attempts to crystallize our thinking about our nation in its centennial, I hope we shall make some attempt to indicate just how Canada has added to the history of the world.
I can remember one professor who often said that Canada gave a pattern by which more people have received freedom than by any other pattern that has been established in this world. He, of course, meant the pattern of the commonwealth; for Canada led all other nations in finding a method by which a colony could become a nation. It perhaps seems strange that when we heard the announcement of the death of the Secretary General of the United Nations this morning, he should have been dealing with this very problem, namely the attempt to find a method by which undeveloped people who have lived in a colonial state may find freedom within a nation state. I think it brings home to us the extent to which Canada can show the pattern by means of which this may be done. I hope this will be one of the things emphasized in our centenary year. I hope we shall not look inward as much as we shall look outward and show others what we have learned.
I think the second great contribution we have made in our history as a nation is to show the world that two different cultures or, as some would have it, two different nations can live within the bosom of a single nation, can co-operate and can find a single consciousness and a single sense of identity within a nation state. Here again, in a world of bloodshed and trouble, I think this is the means by which we can present to the people of the world another area in which Canada has made such great strides. For indeed as we look at other nations, such as South Africa and others too numerous to mention, where the whole problem of national identity is going through a valiant decision, I think Canadian experience can have some real relevance.
In the year of the centennial of confederation I hope we shall do something to dramatize and even to romanticize the great figures in our past history. Perhaps it has been the lot of the prime ministers of our nation to bring forward the contributions of certain men in our past. I am thinking, of course, of men like William Lyon Mackenzie King, who I think gave us a greater realization of the contribution of his famous forebearer, William Lyon Mackenzie. I also think of the efforts of our present Prime Minister to bring about a recognition of the great work of Sir John A. Macdonald. But there are others, such as Lafontaine, Robert Baldwin and

Canadian Centennial
D'Arcy McGee, who virtually gave his life for this nation, who have not been sufficiently dramatized and who are not sufficiently known by the young people of our nation. I think it is to the young people that our efforts should be directed in connection with this centennial, because as yet they have not a sufficient sense of history in spite of what has been done by various branches of government at the federal and provincial levels.
We are heartened by this advance information in connection with the celebration. Perhaps some people may think it strange that it took but three years to create this nation while it has taken seven years to prepare for the celebration of its centenary. However, we live in an age when people are interested in history, and the various facets of Canadian life must be expressed. I can assure the Prime Minister and this government that they can expect the support of all parties in preparing this opportunity to show the world the contributions which Canada has made to the history of mankind.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I wish to say a very few words on this resolution of the right hon. Prime Minister because I am in such wholehearted support of it. The Prime Minister has said that we must plan for much more than just a holiday. He has told us that our founding day as a confederation passed almost without notice, and that John A. Macdonald always regretted this. It may be that if there had been some women in the House of Commons in those days it would not have passed unnoticed, because I think we are much more conscious of anniversaries and celebrations than our male colleagues.
I believe the key word in our centennial celebration should be participation; participation by service clubs, by business organizations, by labour unions, by individuals and by women's clubs. I think one form could be the granting of scholarships, because what an honour it would be for any Canadian to win a centennial scholarship. It certainly would be a once in a lifetime event. There could also be essay contests in Canadian history and in local histories. In Saskatchewan for their jubilee they held an essay contest in local histories. I understand there are now about 3,000 local histories in the Saskatchewan archives. Labour unions might build centennial trade schools, perhaps one in each province. There could be slum clearance contributions by construction companies; literary prizes for books and poems about Canada, perhaps given by press clubs and authors' associations. There are also unlimited opportunities for business organizations.
The Prime Minister has said that the centenary committee has received many suggestions which might cost billions of dollars. Governments alone should not take on these projects or these celebration plans; every Canadian should participate in order to meet the objective voiced by the Prime Minister, which was to stir the imagination of the Canadian people toward national purpose and national unity. I know there will be much pomp and ceremony, parades and gaiety, but let us also celebrate with permanent monuments that will benefit future generations, just as we have benefited from our pioneering forefathers in the spirit and building of Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the Prime Minister very correctly asked for unanimous consent when he presented the motion for this resolution. As far as my limited power is concerned, I am happy to grant him such unanimous approval for the resolution. I think that is generally the wish of the committee of the whole and of the country.
The Prime Minister took advantage of the occasion, very properly again, to make some remarks as to the history of our confederation and the propriety and objectives in celebrating its one hundredth anniversary. I have very few remarks to make. I will have one or two questions later arising out of the resolution itself, but they are purely of a practical nature and arise out of the wording of the resolution itself. This occasion however also provides the opportunity for expressing ideas, and indeed ideals, concerning the celebration of our centennial of confederation. At the same time it is couched in very practical language and in its main provision sets up the corporation that will have administrative responsibility for making the practical arrangements for the occasion and co-ordinating the efforts of others throughout the whole of the country. Therefore at one and the same time we have in this resolution the opportunity to debate the very large, somewhat idealistic question, and also to discuss some of the practical plans for the occasion.
The Associate Minister of National Defence made some remarks which unfortunately I had to listen to after translation. I regret that I was not able to follow them with that precision of understanding that I believe some of them deserve, particularly the latter part of his remarks. I refer to the ideals he was very properly seeking to express, and expressing well.
I wish the associate minister were here, because the earlier part of his remarks was translated in a way that seemed to indicate that a couple of persons only were responsible

for confederation. That idea was quite inconsistent with the main part of the speech and I think may probably be due to the loss of meaning in translation. I merely mention this because it is my understanding of history that confederation was brought about by a great many men of that period who had a wide vision of the future of this country. It was the collective effort of all of them that brought about this great event in our history.
I think we should be very careful not to say or do anything that would in any way detract from that concept of these men, because my whole understanding of history is that had it not been for the co-ordination of effort and the co-operation of all of them, confederation itself would not have been brought about.
I have some further remarks, Mr. Chairman, so perhaps I could call it one o'clock.

speechtext:
When the committee rose for the luncheon adjournment I had not completed my remarks, but since this resolution will, I hope, be unanimously approved I think perhaps it would be as well not to extend my observations unduly or expand them at any great length for fear they might detract somewhat from the unanimity which is certainly desirable.
The development of the proper type of celebration for this occasion will require the participation of great numbers of Canadians, a point which was well taken by the hon. member for York-Humber. It will require the co-ordination of the work of a great many groups and committees throughout the country. Indeed, the more one thinks about it the more one is convinced that it will require a genius to head this organization and guide it in the way it should go, because of necessity there will have to be very close co-operation among provincial groups, provincial committees, local groups and municipal committees. The different points of view which will be put forward will also require co-ordination. The wholly artistic and creative approach will need to be reconciled with a more practical viewpoint in the light of what it is possible to do in a practical way.
I must say that today I extend to the Prime Minister not only good wishes on his birthday, but the hope that he may be blessed with the great skill and wisdom necessary for the wise selection of the personnel he will 90205-6-535J
Canadian Centennial
be appointing in connection with this celebration. This is a task which will require the greatest skill and wisdom. The occasion must be commemorative of the past. That is, of course, elementary. But we must be careful throughout to see that it is inspirational for the future, and that the whole of the celebration throughout the land is ordered in such a way that it will serve as a source of inspiration to those who come long after. This is why it is going to require such wisdom in the appointment of persons able to reconcile the two viewpoints I have mentioned and arrange the functions in a way that is both imaginative and practical.
Some reference has been made by previous speakers to the need for making Canadians aware of Canada; I think this was one of the phrases used. I am in complete accord. As a matter of fact there has been a good deal of discussion of history during the hour or so in which this resolution has been under consideration, and it occurs to me that at this point in our national progress, after making allowance for the economic condition of Canadians as individuals compared with a hundred years ago and after making allowance for the increased travel facilities available, it is probably true to say that we individual Canadians move about our country much less than we should, and know and understand less about other Canadians than we should. I hope that as the work of preparing for this centennial celebration proceeds, a new impetus may be given to the desirability of Canadians moving about Canada a great deal more. Increased importance should be attached to Canadians studying the history and geography of Canada a great deal more so that all of us will have an appreciation of the problems and aspirations of those in other parts of Canada. All Canadians should have a better understanding of the culture, aspirations, habits of life and methods of approaching the problem of living in a civilized society of Canadians in all areas of Canada.
As Canadians we seem in general to be given to travelling to other countries when family units take trips. While that is an excellent thing in itself, I am sometimes appalled at how little Canadians in one part of the country know about the culture, problems and aspirations of those in other parts of the country. I would hope that in the intervening six years as we prepare for the centenary a great deal of added impetus will be given to the study of Canadian history by Canadians, not only in an academic sense through textbooks and cultural programs but in a very real sense through personal contact by moving about the country.

Canadian Centennial
Much has been said about the ethnic groups that form this country, and I am in hearty accord with those remarks. When one analyses it, it seems to me we are really a race of minorities; of great numbers of ethnic groups each with distinctive characteristics and diversified and outstanding cultural attributes. When these centennial programs are initiated across the country, with all Canadians participating, I hope that background will be acknowledged and the programs arranged accordingly. I also hope, however, that running through them we will have the theme that we are now Canadians, and that while we are cherishing and keeping alive the various rich traditions and cultures that have contributed to this nation, we are doing so because they have contributed to our Canadianism, that we are now Canadians one and all, that it is Canada's centenary we are celebrating.
To accomplish this will require infinite tact, discretion and judgement. One adds to the other, as I view the question. In other words the richness of these cultural backgrounds enhances our Canadianism. It is only if these diverse backgrounds are mispresented at public functions that they become separate and detract from our Canadianism. I hope the kind of good judgment required to derive the maximum value from our rich assortment of backgrounds will be used, as I am sure it will be.
As our planning proceeds there will be need to focus the theme of this centennial occasion, and to keep it in focus. I have been reading with a great deal of interest the report of the first annual meeting of the Canadian centenary council in Ottawa on May 12, 1961. I do not know how to adequately describe the material contained in this publication, but perhaps I should draw attention to the reports of program research it contains. They contain an abundance of ideas, most of them excellent. What we must watch in the six years ahead in preparing for the centennial is that these excellent ideas are focused on one great theme.
I hope that in the legislation to be presented some provision will be made to bring this subject matter forward in the House of Commons each year so that hon. members may have an opportunity to express themselves on the direction of the organization, making sure it is focusing on a theme that is worthy of the occasion and is not allowed to become diffused and spread into preparations for a gigantic party celebration for the sake of having a party.
Perhaps the Prime Minister will have something to say on that point, and I hope something can be done in that respect. There are various ways by which this could be

accomplished, including an annual vote by parliament to provide funds, but it is not necessary to elaborate on the means at this time.
I shall now conclude this portion of my remarks. I have one or two questions I wish to direct to the Prime Minister, but I shall reserve them until those who wish to make general remarks on the subject have had an opportunity to do so.
