Even in the short time I have been in the house, I have become cognizant of the fact that he has been' willing to redress little matters of grievance. I should therefore like to mention briefly, if I may, with respect it this legislation some matters to which I think it would he helpful for him to address himself.
Both the minister and the hon. member for York-Scarborough, as I understand it, live in Toronto. The type of riding I represent is very different from those which they represent. This summer I took some time to fly over my riding of Leeds and study it from the air. I could not fail to be impressed by the comparative congestion of the town of Brock-ville and the town of Gananoque with the relatively uncrowded villages. A village like Elgin, for example, which has an extremely fine school, could grow and develop with some sort of assistance. Lansdowne and Athens are two other places that could easily develop with adequate assistance. The town of Smiths Falls which spills into the riding of Leeds to the south must grow in that direction. These places are in my opinion, of the type that could be given some interested scrutiny by the minister.
A riding such as Leeds, which is half urban and half rural, compels certain comparisons. I have been made aware of the fact that our farm population has been declining for approximately 20 years. Not only is that the fact, but these very attractive villages which were to a certain extent the centre of culture some years ago and which were happy places in which to live, have declined in importance rather than grown. I would ask the minister to consider the extent to which this legislation could be made applicable to some of these areas on the fringe of our towns or even in the smaller areas.
My constituents have made me cognizant of the fact that federal housing assistance appears to be available to the town dweller but

not to the country dweller and of the fact that in this regard there is marked disparity. It would be improper within the confines of this debate to spill over into the responsibilities, for example, of the Minister of Agriculture under the Farm Credit Act. However, I think it would be fair to say this. So much red tape is attendant upon getting farm loans that we must perhaps look to our Minister of Public Works for as liberal, broad and generous interpretation as is possible of the provisions of this act.
By people interested in housing and in construction, particularly in the Brockville area, it has been brought to my attention that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation was at first brought into being to promote home building in areas that were unserviced and therefore not acceptable to insurance companies. It was for the purpose of issuing loans to individuals who perhaps could not qualify for insurance company loans. If I am in error in understanding the origins of this act, I am sure I will be corrected. However, in 1961 in the Kingston area we have seen a sharp change with respect to this approach. Now we find rulings which provide that no lot, unless it has services or is in a C.M.H.C. approved subdivision, is acceptable for a C.M.H.C. loan. This, to the thinking of some people very much interested in construction today, would appear to place C.M.H.C. in direct competition with the insurance companies, leaving the former field in which we understand C.M.H.C. was originally particularly interested with no one to look after it.
It seems almost as though in the C.M.H.C. Kingston area a circle has been drawn around a certain point in each town and at various distances out from the limits anyone beyond the perimeter is able to build on his land-for example, with septic systems, septic tanks and tank installations-but beyond that point this is not possible. I of course understand how the minister, whose program involves so many millions of dollars, is urgently concerned about orderly urban development. I can quite appreciate that lack of discipline and lack of orderly growth in this regard could be harmful and damaging. On the other hand I suggest to the minister that there are, particularly in a riding such as mine-which is on the river and extends to the north-many areas which have not been developed at all.
There are places such as Lyndhurst, Elgin, Morton, Delta, and so on, where the persons who live in those villages are for the most part employed in the towns. Many people work in Smiths Falls, Kingston or Brockville and there is not much difference between our countryfolk and our townsfolk. These

are not farmers; they are people enjoying a sort of suburban life. Before the minister simply rejects this suggestion I ask him to consider the possibility of liberalizing to some extent the conditions and requirements of these loans. Every area of ground is different, as we know. There is the problem of sewerage. They are working toward improvement in Gananoque at the present time. I must speak appreciatively of this aspect of assistance to our urban areas.
The Minister of Finance has visited our area. On one occasion in Athens he spoke on behalf of the late Hayden Stanton regarding the requirement of municipalities for greater assistance. This extremely well attended meeting was held in 1957 and his promise of municipal assistance was well received by people who knew something about the burden of municipal financing in our county. I think our municipalities are in a somewhat worse condition today than they were when the Minister of Finance made those suggestions in respect of the assistance to be provided.

We have there a community of 5,000 people who at the present moment are embarking upon a sewerage plan which will probably cost them in the order of $605,000. Without assistance it will be quite impossible for them to carry out this project. It will mean an expense of $121 for every man, woman and child in that small town, which has suffered its share of unemployment in the past two years. I think federal assistance for sewerage development is vitally important.
I also put forward this other point which I hope the minister will appreciate. The purpose of the bill to be founded upon this resolution is to secure parliamentary approval of agreements which have been entered into between the government of Canada and the governments of the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta. These agreements were laid on the table of the house on the 15th of this month by the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Halpenny) and they appear as schedules to the bill. If approved by parliament and by the legislatures of the respective provinces, these agreements will have the effect of terminating the legislative control of the parliament of Canada over the school lands and school lands funds of the three prairie provinces and placing the administration and disposal of those lands and funds within the sole competence of the respective legislatures of those provinces.
The committee may wish to have recalled some of the historical background of the school lands and school lands funds. Under the Dominion Lands Act of 1872, the parliament of Canada set aside two sections of land 90205-6-536J
in each township in Manitoba and the then Northwest Territories as an endowment for education and in the consolidated Dominion Lands Act of 1879 set forth the manner in which this endowment was to be administered by the department of the interior. All sales were to be made by public auction after due advertisement, and at an upset price based upon the fair value of other unoccupied lands in the township. The terms of sale, which have subsequently been changed from time to time, were fixed in 1879 at one fifth in cash and the remainder in nine annual instalments with interest at 6 per cent. The principal arising from the sales was to be invested in dominion securities and the interest arising therefrom as well as the annual revenue from leases, hay permits, etc., on school lands were, after deducting the cost of management of the lands, to be paid annually to the governments of the province or territory within which such lands were situated. The moneys so paid were to be used by the province or territory to support public schools in such manner as the province or territory deemed expedient. In conformity with the above requirements, the government of Canada from 1883, the date of the first sale of school lands, until 1930, when the school lands and school lands funds were transferred to the jurisdiction of the provinces in the natural resources settlement of that year, administered the school lands and school lands funds.
In the agreements which constituted the 1930 natural resources settlement, the three provinces undertook to administer the school lands and the school lands fund they acquired in the settlement, according to the provisions of sections 37 to 40 of the Dominion Lands Act, being chapter 113 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1927. This provision of the natural resources agreements meant that while the provinces had assumed the administration of their school lands and associated funds, the principles on which those lands and funds were to be administered were not to change. The provinces were required to invest the principal from the sale of school lands in a school lands fund and invest the moneys of the fund in securities of Canada.
There have over the years been various representations from one or more of the prairie provinces to have the provisions of the natural resources transfer agreements of 1930 dealing with school lands and the school lands funds amended. As the result of such representations the natural resources transfer agreement with Saskatchewan was amended

Western School Lands Administration in 1948 and in 1951 the transfer agreements with each of the three provinces was amended. The 1948 amendment allowed Saskatchewan to sell school lands to veterans under provisions of the Veterans' Land Act without conforming to the requirement that school lands must only be sold at public auction. The 1951 amendment gave the provinces more latitude as to the securities in which the school lands funds might be invested. The definition of acceptable securities was broadened to include, in addition to securities of Canada, securities of any province, or securities of a municipal corporation or school districts within the province together with securities guaranteed by Canada or a province.
There have been since that time various representations from the prairie provinces that all federal legislative control over their school lands and school lands funds should be removed and the legislatures of the provinces given sole jurisdiction as to the manner of administration or disposal of the lands and the funds. It has been argued that the revenues provided from the school lands are now small in relation to total expenditures on education so that it can scarcely be contended that the maintenance of the funds assures adequate revenues for education.
I have in my hand a brief table relating to school lands funds setting forth the size of funds, expressed in thousands of dollars, the unsold lands, expressed in millions of acres, and the revenues from school lands and school lands funds expressed in thousands of dollars. I seek the unanimous consent of the committee to have this inserted in Hansard at this point.

The situation today is this. The revenues from school lands as a percentage of provincial expenditure on education declined in Manitoba from 9.5 per cent in 1945-46 to 3.5 per cent in 1957-58. In Saskatchewan, the revenues from school lands were 21.9 per cent of educational expenditures in 1945-46 and 14.2 per cent in 1958-59. The provinces have also contended that the retention of federal control over the use of the school lands and school lands funds in the three prairie provinces infringes upon their autonomy and that the existence of this legislative control involves unnecessary administrative work and impairs the financial flexibility of the provinces concerned. In the belief that the arguments advanced by the provinces were reasonable and in the desire to co-operate with the prairie provinces in this matter, the Prime Minister at the dominion-provincial conference of February 1961, suggested that the governments of Canada, Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta should enter into an agreement to confer on those provinces complete authority over their school lands and their school lands funds. The provinces were agreeable to such an arrangement and agreements to this effect have been entered into by the governments concerned. The house will be asked by the bill to be founded upon this resolution to approve on behalf of Canada the agreements entered into with the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta. The agreements as I said will become effective when they have also been approved by the legislatures of the provinces concerned.

Mr. Chairman, as the parliamentary secretary has indicated we are discussing an amendment to section 7 of the basic agreement between the federal government and the three prairie provinces entered into in 1930, removing any suggestion that these funds are to be regarded as trust funds and specially segregated and under special

Western School Lands Administration
rules in so far as income therefrom is concerned in the hands of the provincial governments.
I do not think the amendment to the original agreement that will likely appear in the bill will prove to be nearly as controversial or delaying in debate as was the original amendment introduced by the Mackenzie King government in 1930.
At that time the opposition of the day suggested that, notwithstanding that the agreement seemed to eliminate a long standing controversy and sense of grievance that existed in the prairie provinces because they did not appear to be on a similar basis as were the other provinces of Canada with respect to their natural resources under section 109, I believe, of the original British North America Act of 1867, and quite apart from any infringement of autonomy with respect to school lands, there were none the less other infringements of autonomy unlike the conditions that applied with respect to the natural resources of the older provinces. It was suggested that the federal government retained certain rights with respect to lands in which it had made investments for national parks, including mineral rights with respect thereto. Certain suggestions were made to the effect that there were also some restrictions on the prairie provinces with respect to water development unlike the situation in the older provinces. There was also the suggestion that by the retention of some federal rights with respect to lands that had already been designated as Indian reserves, the amendment of 1930 was unsatisfactory.
I wonder whether, as a result of the recent negotiations with these provinces which result in the present amendments to the 1930 agreement, the prairie provinces have indicated that they seek changes in the areas I have outlined and in the area of control of national parks. Of course, if control were to be released they might also seek control with respect to expenditures in relation to those territories designated as parks. Perhaps this control would fall to the provinces ipso facto. speakeroldname: Hon. Leon Balcer (Minister of Transport) moved
subsubtopic: CONSTRUCTION OF LINE TO GREAT SLAVE LAKE
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-126, respecting the construction of a line of railway in the province of Alberta and in the Northwest Territories by Canadian National Railway Company from a point at or near Grimshaw, in the province of Alberta, in a northerly direction to Great Slave lake, in the northwest territories.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the bill which we now have before us is an important and long

awaited step in the development of the north, but more particularly in that portion of the Northwest Territories tributary to Great Slave lake.
Authority is being sought to enable the Canadian National Railways to build a branch line from Grimshaw, Alberta, to Great Slave lake, Northwest Territories, a distance of approximately 438 miles, under which the government will advance to the company the funds required for the construction of the line but not exceeding $86,250,000. This sum represents a preliminary estimate of the cost of construction of $75 million plus 15 per cent for contingencies.
As hon. members know, a survey of the route is in progress and is expected to be completed by the end of the year. Only then will it be possible to make a detailed and realistic estimate of costs. If it should develop that unforeseen construction difficulties should increase the costs beyond those presently estimated, then additional funds would have to be provided.
It is over 30 years since the settlers north of Grimshaw were promised an immediate extension of the Northern Alberta Railway to the northern boundary of Alberta. However, little serious interest was shown in the matter until 1954, when the existence of a major zinc-lead ore body at Pine Point was confirmed.
Following this development there were repeated intermittent discussions between the federal government and Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company regarding the need for a railway to Great Slave lake. The royal commission on Canada's economic prospects also received representations in 1955 and 1956 on behalf of the Northwest Territories which emphasized the need for such a railway, but the commission dealt with the matter in a general and indefinite way.
The throne speech of May 1958, included the statement that in order to promote national development on the frontier in the north, parliament would be asked to authorize the construction of a railway to Great Slave lake. A wide divergence of opinion immediately developed as to the route which should be followed by the proposed railway and a royal commission was appointed in June 1959, to inquire into the matter and to report to parliament. The report of the commission became available in July 1960, with the majority opinion favouring the western route from Grimshaw. In keeping with this opinion it was announced in November 1960, in the speech from the throne, that a detailed survey of the western route would be undertaken; and in December 1960, when $250,000 was appropriated to start the survey, I stated in the house that a railway would be built on
Canadian National Railways this route after the completion of the survey. In February 1961, I further stated that, because of the distance involved, the proposed line could not be self supporting from the start so that some form of governmental subvention would be necessary.
The proposed railway extension from Grimshaw will follow a route paralleling the Mackenzie highway and terminating at the port of Hay River. A spur line from the vicinity of Alexander Falls, some 25 miles south of Hay River, will serve the needs of Pine Point mine. Some might ask "Why build a railway when a highway is available", the suggestion being that the Pine Point mine might be brought into production on the basis of trucking. That possibility has been explored and we are satisfied that rail transport offers the more economical means of bringing the property into production as well as furthering the development of the north.
Construction of the railway line will bring about major new construction projects, namely a $21 million mining camp at Pine Point; a $16 million expansion of the plant of Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company at Trail, B.C; a $2 million community development at Pine Point; and some $5 million for new railway equipment and rehabilitation of existing railways. The total capital expenditure involved, including the $75 million estimated cost for the new line, will thus total about $120 million.
The operation of Pine Point mines will result in the annual production and shipment of some 215,000 tons of lead and zinc concentrates. As I indicated at the resolution stage, if the Pine Point operation was not undertaken, the Canadian economy would be adversely affected not only by the substantial loss in employment but by the necessity of importing foreign concentrates at a cost of about $13 million annually to maintain the output of the Trail plants. Moreover, under these circumstances, Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company would not expand its plant at Trail so that additional export business from the sale of metal amounting to about $6 million per year would not be obtained.
While the Pine Point mining operations would be the most important immediate development resulting from the construction of the proposed railway, other important benefits would also be realized. I outlined some of them at the resolution stage, namely provision of service to some 8,000 people living north of Grimshaw; provision of service to existing industries such as commercial fishing on Great Slave lake and gold mining at Yellowknife; stimulation of agricultural expansion

Canadian National Railways in some 6 million acres of arable land adjacent to the railway; stimulation of forest industries based on some 13 million acres of adjacent forest lands; and stimulation of mineral exploration. In other words, the proposed railway would be somewhat different from most branch lines constructed in recent years which were designed to service one mine or a group of mines. Its purpose, in fact, is to open up a whole new region.
The Great Slave lake railway will therefore be for the general development of the north. A substantial freight movement will immediately be generated by the operation of Pine Point Mines Limited. It is estimated that this movement will result in total revenues of some $5 million annually from the shipment of concentrates southward from Pine Point and the shipment of supplies north to Pine Point. The portion of this revenue accruing to the new section of the line would be about $1,700,000 annually. In addition, the report of the royal commission on the Great Slave lake railway estimates that existing business in the area would provide a further $1,200,000 annually. Total revenues available to the new section of the line would thus approximate $2,900,000 per year.
Thus a considerable traffic will be carried over the line although not all of this can be expected to accrue immediately. For this reason we felt that some financial assistance from the mining company was required in view of the indispensability of the railway to the new mining development at Pine Point.
I am happy to state that it has been possible to reach an agreement with the companies concerned, namely Consolidated Mining and Smelting and its subsidiary, Pine Point Mines, respecting the amount of assistance to be extended by the companies and the conditions under which it is to be payable.
I should like to review the principal terms briefly. To provide sufficient flexibility in the discharging of the agreement provision has been made for varying rates of production at the mine and for varying levels of earnings of the railway, and the over-all results are averaged out over the period of the agreement.
The basic terms are:
(1)	The railway is to be completed on or before December 31, 1966.

Continuing the basic terms, they are:
(2)	The mine is to be in production on or before the same date.
(3)	The mining company is to pay a rate of $7.75 per ton on all ores or concentrates shipped up to 215,000 tons annually for the first 10 years of operation. Normal rates which are less than $7.75 per ton will be paid on traffic in excess of 215,000 tons in any year provided the cumulative shipments in previous years have averaged 215,000 tons or more annually.
(4)	In addition, the mining company will pay a special transportation charge, based on the value of the concentrates shipped, starting three years after the commencement of production and extending for 10 years. This will not exceed $2 million in any year and $20 million over the whole 10-year period. At the anticipated rate of production and at the average lead and zinc prices prevailing during the period 1951 to 1960 this contribution would aggregate $12,500,000 over the 10 years. This amount is to be payable to the railway, which will in turn pay it to the government. It constitutes a capital contribution of the mining company toward the building of the railway.
(5)	There are additional terms in the agreement which provide for the handling of current deficiencies or surpluses in the level of railway revenues during the 10-year period and safeguard the position of Canadian National Railways so that any reduction in the volume of mine traffic will not result in an operating deficit to be borne by the railway. The railway undertakes that no other producers of ores or concentrates on its line will receive any more favourable terms than those accorded Pine Point Mines.
The agreement also provides for the routing of the ores and concentrates traffic between Pine Point Mines and Tadanac, British Columbia, and the west coast so that each of the participating carriers will receive an equitable share of the traffic.
In summary, the advantages of constructing the proposed railway are very great:
(1)	It will implement an essential element of the government's announced program of northern development.
(2)	It will have a pronounced stimulating effect in all parts of the Mackenzie area.
(3)	It will avoid the importation of zinc concentrates and effect a substantial saving in foreign exchange.
(4)	It will bring about substantial employment, both in construction of the railway and in construction of the new mine at Pine Point, including the new community there, and expanded facilities at Trail, B.C. These projects will require about four years to complete and over that period employment for several hundred men will be provided.

In the light of all considerations the government believes the proposal is a sound one and I trust it will commend itself to all hon. members. When the bill has been given second reading I propose to move that it be referred to the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines.

Mr. Speaker, I have listened carefully to the interesting statement made by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Balcer) in connection with the construction of this Pine Point line from Grimshaw to Great Slave lake. We on this side of the house support this bill, as I stated during the discussion at the resolution stage. We support it for many reasons. First, because-and I need not repeat what I said at that time, except in a very general way-it was the former administration that recommended the construction of this line together with a whole program for the development of the northern part of Canada to the royal commission on economic prospects in November, 1955. I dealt with some of the details of the brief which was presented to the commission on that date by Mr. R. J. Robertson, the commissioner of the Northwest Territories as he then was.
I think I also indicated at the time that we favoured the construction of this, a developmental line, because not only would it assist in moving strategic material from the area in the Great Slave lake, but it would also assist intermediate traffic between that point and Grimshaw and Edmonton.
In the course of his statement a moment ago the minister added a number of very important reasons why parliament should approve the construction of this line. However, I hope the minister will not feel that the criticism I intend to make now is criticism againt the principle of this measure. Rather it is criticism of the manner in which the government has proceeded.
We think, sir, the government has put the cart before the horse in this case and that this is an example of another Columbia river project. In other words, that long before the agreement among the four parties, namely Her Majesty, Canadian National Railways, Consolidated Mining and Smelting and Pine Point Mines was signed, executed and completed, parliament was asked to deal with this measure first by way of resolution and then by way of a bill.
On July 1 I put the following question to the Prime Minister:
Could I ask the Prime Minister whether the agreement referred to in the resolution which appeared on the order paper yesterday among the Canadian National Railways, the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company of Canada and the Pine Point Mines Limited has been negotiated and signed by the parties involved in this bill?

Canadian National Railways great developmental project for natural resources has been executed but agreement with the province of British Columbia, the one concerned, has not been brought forward. Today the case is the same.
I want to say a word or two about the route. After four years the government has decided to follow the Grimshaw-Great Slave lake route. The minister himself told the sad story. Here is what he said: In 1958 here is what the government said in the speech from the throne: "Parliament will be asked to authorize the construction of the Pine Point railway". In 1959 a royal commission was established to select a route, to decide whether it should be the eastern route by way of Waterways or the western route through Grimshaw. In 1960 the report of the royal commission was available favouring the Grimshaw route. In 1961, the minister announced that the line would be self supporting.
The question I put to the minister is this: did not the officials of his department-I shall not accuse him, of course, because he was not the minister then-did not the officials of his department know that this was the best route to follow long before the speech from the throne of 1958 was prepared? Is there no evidence in the files of the department to indicate that the Grimshaw route was the one favoured by the authorities in the department? I think parliament is entitled to know that. If that is the case, why did the government wait four years before bringing about this legislation when it had in its flies a recommendation, so I understand- if I am wrong the minister will correct me- to the effect that the Grimshaw route was more suitable from the point of view of terrain and should be followed? None the less there has been all this delay because, we are informed, the government favoured the Waterways route and hoped and expected that the royal commission would report unanimously or at least in the majority in favour of the Waterways route. I think the house is entitled to get some clarification on that point from the minister.
Then I think we should hear something about the cost. Is there anything in the files of the department to indicate what the cost of this project was going to be when the government took office in 1957? I think we should be told. The information which has been brought to my attention is that the line would have cost between $50 million and $55 million. If this is the case, the house is entitled to an explanation of why there has been an increase to $86 million.
Then we are entitled to know whether the taxpayers of Canada will get their capital back. Is this line going to be economic in the
[Mr. Chevrier.l
light of the traffic which will move from the mines and the intermediate points? Then again, where will the traffic go after it reaches Edmonton; how will it be divided between the railways?
Of course, the minister has outlined in some detail what is contained in the agreement but does he not think we should be shown the agreement before we dispose of a matter of this importance? After all, I am sure the minister is anxious to get this legislation through. This is good legislation in principle. He should give the house all the information available so that the opposition may be in possession of the same information as he has in order to be able to pass judgment on whether the agreement is one which is beneficial to the crown interests and those of the taxpayer. Mr. Speaker, as I said when speaking to the resolution we support the principle of the bill because it provides for transportation that will serve the settlers in this area as well as meet the needs of the present development there. Without doubt it will also promote further development. However, it is quite obvious that the possibility of the construction of the railroad is based almost entirely upon the Pine Point development and its stability and future.
Before proceeding with my remarks in that connection I wish to bring to the attention of the house the fact that we have here another instance of the Canadian Pacific Railway failing to assume its responsibility. It refuses to build a railroad to its own mine. That is a matter of fact. Pine Point Mines Limited is owned by Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company of Canada Limited and the C.P.R. is the major owner of Consolidated Mining and Smelting.
Like the previous speaker I express regret at the fact that the house is being asked to deal with this legislation without a copy of a completed and signed agreement. We are dealing with it with the feeling that there are uncertainties of which we would not have knowledge at this time with respect to this agreement.
I have followed this development with a great deal of interest because I represent a constituency in which Consolidated Mining and Smelting is the largest industrial operation. I am always interested in their activities both industrial and otherwise. I have had much correspondence with mining engineers and have held conversations with engineers connected with mines in the Kootenays, and so on that account I have amassed a considerable amount of information on the subject. I shall deal with only one aspect of the proposal this evening. The construction of this line is based almost entirely on the stability and future of Pine Point Mines Limited.
I have in my hand an extract from the May 1954 Canadian Mining Journal which I wish to place on the record. I always tend to cock an eye with respect to mining prospects. I have lived in mining country all my life. I have noticed an inclination on the part of those engaged in this industry to be too optimistic with respect to future development. I shall quote a few extracts from various sources to indicate the variation in the estimates of the ore reserves connected with Pine Point Mines Limited.
90205-6-537i
Canadian National Railways
The journal to which I referred points out:
Thus the tonnage of indicated ore has been expanded from the 500,000 tons reported in 1930 to several million tons. This testing has been concentrated in the shallower eastern part of the property, and as a result about two thirds of the indicated ore can be mined by open pit methods.
I turn now to the 1960 issue of the Canadian Mines Handbook which refers to the fact that churn drilling at Pine Point Mines Limited has outlined several million tons of ore of which approximately 50 per cent is minable by open pit methods.
I deal now with a report published by the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources entitled "Known Mineralized Areas and Mining Development-Yukon Territory and Northwest Territories" prepared by K. J. Christie, B.Sc., P.Eng. head, mining section, resources division, northern administration branch, in which he has the following to say:
Some of the world's largest deposits of lead and zinc have been found in this type of deposit and it would appear that Pine Point is not an exception. Although the company does not state the amount of ore reserves, the generally accepted figure is in excess of 10 million tons.
He then goes on to deal with the possibilities for the development of this ore.
The Financial Post of April 4, 1960 carried an article entitled "Push Railways to Catch Vote". That is a rather unkind implication, is it not? In this article I read:
The Pine Point deposit contains 5 million tons of 7.4 per cent zinc ore which could be mined on an open pit basis and milled on the spot for Cominco Trail, B.C., smelter.
I turn now to the report of the annual meeting of the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company of Canada held on April 28, 1960 at Montreal, in which is contained the address to shareholders of the president, Mr. W. S. Kirkpatrick. Mr. Kirkpatrick had this to say:
At the annual meeting in 1940 Sir Edward Beatty, then chairman of the company, remarked that ore reserves at the Sullivan were sufficient for well over 20 years of operation at the existing rate of production. The same statement can be made today after 20 years of continuous production at rates between 2 and 3 million tons of ore per year.
He went on to say:
Therefore, while operation at the present rate of 21 million tons annually is assured for many years, it would not be sound practice to attempt to satisfy our full smelter capacity by increasing the output from the Sullivan .. . The most important result has been the Pine Point discovery at Great Slave lake where work completed in 1954 indicates reserves of the same general order as those at the Sullivan.
I come now to the address of Mr. Kirkpatrick to the annual meeting of the shareholders which was held on April 27, 1961, in which he says:

Canadian National Railways
In my address last year I touched on the subject of ore reserves, and I wish to discuss this further today.
This is an interesting point:
It has not been the practice of the company to report ore reserves in terms of tons and grade because we feel that such information is commonly misinterpreted.
While our mining plan sets out our program for the next 25 years, this does not define the extent of Sullivan ore reserves, and I can assure you that the mine is good for many decades at the present rate of output.
Anyway, here is a company indicating that it does not report its ore reserves in terms of tons and grade. I just make that point at the present time.
This is part of an article which appeared in Collier's magazine for August 9, 1952:
Just across the lake at Pine Point, Consolidated Mining and Smelting is sinking an exploratory shaft this year into what is believed to be the world's largest body of lead and zinc. Diamond drilling indicates that the ore is a 200 foot chunk, almost flat, and parallels the surface over an area 20 miles long and two miles wide.
It goes on with further details. In Maclean's magazine of March 31, 1956, we find this article in connection with this subject:
There seems to be no shortage of future Canadian economic milestones. One of the world's largest lead-zinc deposits has been outlined at Pine Point, on the south shore of Great Slave lake. The ore body is reported to be 36 miles long, three miles wide and up to 100 feet thick.
In Maclean's magazine of November 15, 1954, there is an article dealing with the same subject in which the following appears:
The ore bodies run for 36 miles in a three mile strip. The most conservative figure places the potential at 120 million tons.
I come to an address by Mr. R. H. Dean of Nesbitt, Thompson and Company Limited, in which he deals with this question as follows:
Extension of rail some 400 miles north to Great Slave lake has been recommended by the commissioner of the Northwest Territories to hasten mineral development, particularly at Pine Point, said to have in excess of 600 million tons of ore containing lead and zinc, and awaiting early development by private industry.
At the convention of the mining institute of Canada, held at Edmonton in 1958, Mr. R. H. Dean is reported to have told the convention that the deposit was "said to have in excess of 600 million tons". We find that attending the conference was Mr. W. G. Jewett, vice president of Cominco, in charge of mines. According to this report he did not question Mr. Dean's estimate.
I mention these various reports and these articles in periodicals, Mr. Speaker, to indicate what a wide variation there is in the assessment of the reserves at Pine Point. I trust that when this bill goes before the committee the officials of the Department of

Mines and Technical Surveys will have some accurate information to give the committee so that it will know it has a sound basis on which to support this bill so far as the stability of the future production of Pine Point Mines is concerned.
According to the bill, this could cost the public $86,250,000. Hon. members have to justify that expenditure of public money. This matter should be very carefully considered by the committee. The officers of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys should be heard. They have the information because they have issued reports on this mine. The officers of the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company, and the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Pacific Railway should be heard. It would be a wise thing for the committee to invite representatives from the Canadian institute of mining, and other witnesses who wish to attend. It is essential that the committee have all the facts available when it is discussing this question.
As the previous speaker said, the committee and the house are entitled to know whether the mine is going to be profitable. If it is not, we should be frank and tell the public that it must expect to lose a certain amount of money each year for a number of years in order to promote this development and in order to relieve the Canadian Pacific Railway of a responsibility which in the first instance is theirs. Then, they should give the final details of this agreement; otherwise, as the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Che-vrier) said, we might be endorsing a sort of second Columbia treaty which we find is not quite what we expected it to be when it was brought to our attention in the house.
Another point the committee should inquire into is how is this $20 million going to be paid by the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company and the Pine Point Mines Limited. The committee should also be entitled to know whether the companies concerned are permitted to deduct expenditures made in this direction, or to include them as costs of operation and benefit from income tax deductions so that in the final analysis the country would never receive a very large percentage of the $20 million which may seem somewhat attractive in the bill at the present time.
There are numerous other details. This is an important matter. The committee has to give the bill very close study indeed so that when they return to their constituencies the members will be able to justify supporting this subsidy of possibly up to $86,250,000.
I have read some of these agreements with large companies in Canada and I can say

quite truthfully that in Canada some large companies have received very large concessions from the government of Canada on information given to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) that was proven not to be true, and we can prove it. I think we must have all these details explained in order to understand the situation, the possibilities for expansion and development, the costs involved, the costs of maintenance and the situation the Canadian National Railways is likely to face in the years ahead.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, after being in this house for some years it is still a matter of amazement to me to observe the way in which the opposition parties persist in beating their weary, wounded, bloody heads against the stone wall of facts. I expect this of the party which sits to your immediate left, Mr. Speaker. Politically speaking they have the kind of head which is designed by nature for pushing up against stone walls. I feel sorry for members of the official opposition who really should know better. On several occasions, either in the house or in committee, I have placed before hon. members incontrovertible facts which I suggest are not capable of successful contradiction and which members of the opposition have not attempted to contradict, to explain and set out in words of one syllable, which they should be able to understand, that any delay which has been caused to the bringing about of this great national project can be attributed entirely to their actions.
I was glad to note that the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) during the course of his remarks said he favoured the principle of this bill, but then he made a great number of exceptions. He referred to a four year delay. The memoranda to which he referred and which contained the brief filed by Mr. Robertson, the deputy minister of northern affairs in 1955 before the Gordon commission, did in truth say that they favoured the construction of this railway. The brief went on to make it manifestly clear that the route which was favoured was the western route. Attached to that brief was a map which outlined the route proposed to be followed, and it was similar to the one the present government now proposes.
However, it is my submission, and I have placed the facts on the record from time to time to prove this, that from that time on the feelings of the then government changed for some reason or other. I have never been able to ascertain the reason, but they decided to proceed with the construction, if at all, by the eastern route.
Canadian National Railways

subsubtopic: CONSTRUCTION OF LINE TO GREAT SLAVE LAKE
speechtext: That is just in your mind, but it might be so.

subsubtopic: CONSTRUCTION OF LINE TO GREAT SLAVE LAKE
speechtext:
I am prepared to show the hon. member at any time that these are the facts and they cannot be controverted. This was the view of the then government. They may have held that view through ignorance or they might have been interested in helping their friends. There might have been many reasons, but that was their intention. This was the situation when the present government came into office. The government, under the leadership of the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker), might have acted in an arbitrary and arrogant way. They might have said, we have certain records here and recommendations; we are going to build this railroad by the eastern or McMurray route. Instead of doing that, when it was brought to the attention of the members of the government that there was a logical and just reason for the construction of the western route, when it was made apparent that there were people who had a claim, in equity, to being considered, when the economics of construction and operation and of the potential traffic which might be generated were made plain, the government appointed a royal commission to consider the matter rather than have it debated in the partisan and heated atmosphere of this chamber.
Evidence was given by the various municipalities, private companies, private individuals and groups, and the hearings of that commission occupied a period of more than a year. Although the commission was set up in June, 1959, it was not until July, 1960 that a report was made. The government, as indicated by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Balcer), then properly saw fit to accept the majority recommendations of that report and at the ensuing session of parliament included in the speech from the throne a statement to the effect that a location survey would be made. I believe effect was given to this intention some time in December. I recall going home to my constituency during the Christmas recess last year and finding that the people and equipment of the Canadian National Railways were then poised and ready, waiting for this house to pass the appropriation. They went to work at once and I believe the survey will be brought to a conclusion some time at the end of this year.
We have a proceeding in our profession known as estoppel. I suggest that the official opposition should be estopped from ever suggesting that any of this delay could be laid at the door of the existing government. They, and they alone must accept the responsibility.
Now, Mr. Speaker, some question has arisen as to the signing of the agreement. I think I can well leave that question to the minister,

Canadian National Railways but I can make this remark. I think it was essential that there be a survey. I believe some consideration must be given to the question of costs, to the question of grades and the operating costs of this railroad. I believe that question will not be completely answered until the survey is completed. However, I am satisfied in my own mind that enough information is now available to permit the parties to have some idea of what those figures will be.
I believe the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) is entirely incorrect when he says that this railroad is being constructed entirely for the Pine Point developers. I will agree it is a fact that the existence of this large ore body at Pine Point ensures, as I have said before, the bread and butter costs of operating the railroad for the first few years. It might well be difficult to justify the immediate construction of the road without this ore body. However, I deny absolutely that it constitutes the entire reason for construction. The minister mentioned something about 8,000 people living north of Grimshaw. I think the census concluded this year will indicate that the number is nearer 18,000 or 20,000. These people are the descendents of those who settled here many, many years ago and who were promised that, in due course, a railroad would be provided for them.
As I have said, it might be difficult to justify the costs which are envisaged by this measure if it were for the convenience of these people alone. However, when we find there is a more cogent reason, when we find that there is another reason economically for the railroad being built, surely under those circumstances it would be improper and unjust to build the railroad without regard to the promise to these people that a railroad would be constructed in due course. I propose, if I have the time, to say something to indicate what the resources are in this area in addition to Pine Point. I am not exaggerating when I say that long after Pine Point is forgotten there will be in the area which is tributary to this railway, settlements consisting of hundreds of thousands of people producing goods, commodities and services bearing no relationship at all to the mining properties at Pine Point.
Pine Point itself, Mr. Speaker, is something of an anomaly. It is found, not in the pre-Cambrian shield where so many of the mining properties in Canada have been discovered, but in a sedimentary basin many miles to the west. Extraordinarily enough, it was discovered in 1898 by prospectors who were travelling into the Yukon. Attempts were made from time to time to delineate the area of this particular ore body, but it was not until the last 10 or 15 years when

Consolidated Mining and Smelting, through its subsidiary Pine Point mines, continued studies and undertook the development and exploration work necessary that the ore body was delineated.
The hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) made some reference to a speech made by Mr. Kirkpatrick, the president of Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company, in dealing with this particular mine. If he had read a little further-and I give him credit that he did not read one of the truly pertinent parts of this speech-I think he would have found there significant facts which answered any questions he asked. This is what Mr. Kirkpatrick said in his speech. It may possibly not be the same speech to which the hon. member referred. The speech I have is one made by Mr. Kirkpatrick before the Alberta and northwest chamber of mines and resources at Edmonton on January 13,
1961.	Here is what Mr. Kirkpatrick said at that time:
The first claims in the Pine Point area were staked in 1898 by miners on their way to the Klondike. This find lay dormant until about 1916 when more exploration work was done. There was renewed activity around 1920, but again nothing came of it. About 1928, interest in the area was revived, and a program of drilling and shaft sinking was undertaken, but when the depression came the project was abandoned. It was not until 1948, 50 years after the original staking, that my company initiated a systematic program of exploration under a three year concession. As a result of this work, new claims were staked, and in 1951, Pine Point Mines Limited was incorporated to continue the development. By the end of 1954, and after the expenditure of some $3 million, the existence of large reserves of zinc-lead ore was established. Grade and other conditions were satisfactory for a mining operation, and tests had demonstrated that high grade concentrates could be produced.
As I indicated in my address to Cominco shareholders last April,-
That may well be the speech to which the hon. member referred.
-the Sullivan mine at Kimberley, B.C. now provides about two third of Cominco's lead and zinc, and can continue to produce at this rate for several decades to come. However-
And this is what I want to emphasize to the house.
-certain physical conditions in the mine limit the rate at which ore can be extracted, and we have been operating at the maximum economic limit for some years. Of course, in times of emergency, as during world war II, higher rates of production can be maintained for limited periods.
Certain other sources of Cominco metal are becoming depleted, particularly a large stockpile of residue material which will be exhausted in
1962.	In order that we may utilize the reserves of our various mines in the most economic manner, new sources of supply are needed both to maintain the present output of our reduction plants and to increase the output as required by expanding market opportunities.
The initial rate of operation proposed at Pine Point would result in an increase in the output of

refined metal from the Trail plants. In our opinion, it will be possible to dispose of this additional output by the time the mine can be brought into operation. For the more distant future, our longterm forecasts indicate that growing world consumption of lead and zinc will create growing opportunities for metal from Canadian mines.
Here may I interject that those who are familiar with the Paley report which is a projection of the material requirements of the North American continent made some years ago and projected to the end of 1975, and who have had the opportunity to study the reports or who have watched the progress made in the light of the Paley report, will agree with the statements which I think can be inferred from Mr. Kirkpatrick's address, namely that in the long term future lead and zinc from our country have a very considerable place in the world commodities market. Then Mr. Kirkpatrick goes on to say this:
However, it should be noted that, in view of the known resources of ore throughout the world, in relation to expected consumption, we do not anticipate a return to the peak metal prices obtained from time to time during the early 1950's .. .
To prepare for the proposed operations at Pine Point, and to extend the Trail plants to treat all resulting concentrates, will require direct investment by Pine Point Mines Limited and Cominco estimated to total in the order of $40 million.
That is very much along the lines mentioned by the minister. As the minister has intimated, by giving the analysis of the agreement, I do not think this large company is prepared to spend some $20 million for the railway and $40 million in development unless it has a fairly good assurance that it has a sufficient ore body there, that it requires the produce from the ore body at its Sullivan mine to make this a sound and economic operation, and not only for the purpose of enhancing to some extent existing operations but certainly to make sure that they are carried on in an economic way.
I personally do not hold any special brief for the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company or for Pine Point Mines nor am I opposed. Large commercial concerns must be expected, I suppose, as one of the byproducts of our system but if kept within the bounds of propriety and good management, they must be accepted. But certainly this company, having expended this money, having opened up this property, having indicated its willingness to make these further expenditures, I think it is good business on the part of the government of Canada to make sure this is done by proceeding, as it has done, within the four corners of the bill.
Before I leave this matter there is one other subject I should like to discuss with regard to the Pine Point operation. I recognize the fact that at the present time it is
Canadian National Railways probably essential that the operations of the mine should be limited to mining and the shipment of concentrates to Trail. However, I hope that in the not too distant future, after proper consideration has been given to the economics of transportation as regards the shipment of concentrates as opposed to the shipment of finished product from the smelter, this company itself might well give some consideration to the establishment of a smelter at Pine Point. This could mean a city of some 15,000 to 25,000 people. At a time when unfortunately we have lagged so far behind the Soviet union in its program of northern development, I would think it most desirable, wherever possible, that through a reasonable measure of decentralization we should work towards the establishment of concentrations of population in the north. If we are going to keep this north country of ours we shall have to make sure that it does not go by default. The establishment of such a smelter might have some effect in accelerating and expanding further explorations in the Northwest Territories so that mine operations which might have otherwise been uneconomical because of the necessity for the shipment of concentrates over a great distance, might well come over the borderline and become economic if there is a custom smelter at Pine Point. I make my submission at this time so that it may in the future receive some consideration.
I mention the fact that there were other aspects of this railway in addition to the mining operation at Pine Point. It was my pleasure to be home during the brief summer recess. Owing to the fact that my constituency covers almost a third of the province of Alberta, I was not able to get around as much as I should have liked. However, I made it a point to go to Pine Point, the Mackenzie highway and into Yellowknife, with particular regard to the impact the proposal to build this railroad was having and would have in the future on northern development. I found there a spirit of optimism. We in the north like to think we have more optimism than others. We like to think that we are the country of tomorrow more than is any other part of Canada. I found that spirit more prevalent today not only because of the wonderful crop we have had but because of the fact that the people of my country have now learned that there, at long last, is a government prepared to give effect to their aspirations and their logical and legitimate request, and which has decided firmly and irrevocably to proceed with this great project. I found up and down the Mackenzie highway evidence of new businesses which had come

Canadian National Railways into existence, indications that new communities will spring up. Farmers who have existed for many years faced with the prospect of having to haul their produce hundreds of miles now see a railroad coming close to them. I spoke to one farmer who told me he went up there 35 years ago waiting for this railroad. Today the survey stakes pass within one half mile of his window. He told me that each day he walks out to examine these stakes. To him this is a dream come true, or a pledge redeemed.
This country offers a potential in agriculture far beyond what was ever conceived. I had an opportunity to speak to the management of one of the experimental farms in our area which has been conducting a most interesting innovation in connection with the provision of community pasture. Nobody yet knows what is the true potential acreage of agriculture in the area which will be tributary to this railway. The best figures I have been able to obtain coincide somewhat with those given by the minister, that there are somewhere between 6 million and 8 million acres of arable land, some 4 million to 5 million acres of what is called doubtful arable land, and some 15 million or 16 million acres of what is described as bush or woodland.
If this innovation which has been carried out by the experimental farm proves successful-and I saw evidence to indicate that it will be-then what I saw leads me to the firm conclusion that there is available in this district north of Grimshaw millions of acres of land which could provide summer pasturage for great herds of cattle. We have just passed through a very difficult period of drought in western Canada. In the light of the expanding population, in the light of the requirements of our people and of the peoples of other parts of the world, it is my firm belief that in the future the country which lies north of Grimshaw will, on the basis of the livestock population, provide an area of settlement and development for many, many thousands of farmers.
I suppose I may be accused of being naive and of making arguments which are farfetched, but when we hear talk at this time of many billions of dollars being expended in weapons of destruction I think it is a mark of courage, a mark of significance that our government is prepared at this time to pledge its belief in the future by this comparatively modest contribution. I say that because the contribution is modest in the light of the moneys which are being voted by other governments for purposes of destruction. It is a mark of courage and significance to open up this great area lying between Grimshaw and Great Slave lake so that the agricultural products, the products of the

lakes and of the forests will be available to be devoted in the interests of peace when we have learned to adapt and fashion our methods of trade so that the unaligned nations will be the recipients of this produce.
I think it is significant that today when the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Diefen-baker) had occasion to speak about the centennial, he made several observations which to me are quite important in relating to this particular bill. The Prime Minister referred to what happened during 1867 and shortly thereafter-the march to the west. I think it would be remarkably significant and related to our centennial observations if, when we come to observe them in 1967, we find we have come to the point where because of the march to the north we have added to Canada the equivalent of another vast empire of productivity. This railroad, I submit-and I think it will be shown-will be the catalyst which will bring it about. This will probably be one of the brightest jewels in the diadem of our centennial observations.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is not for me a local issue. It is a national issue because it involves progress on a level comparable to those large national developments which have concerned us in more recent days. I refer to the St. Lawrence seaway, the Cape Breton causeway, the Kitimat development, projects that are to be compared with those that concern Canada today in the Saskatchewan dam, and some other developments to which people in parliament have devoted their attention on a national basis.
I am prompted to make a few remarks tonight upon second reading of this bill because I talked within the last few days to one who had a very personal interest in it. I refer to our esteemed colleague, the hon. member for Mackenzie River (Mr. Hardie) who unfortunately is not able to be with us. He is one of those who wanted to see an advance of this kind develop post haste, without too much controversy perhaps as to route.
I felt that the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) was always capable of making a very good speech. However, I must say I thought he spoke tonight with some embarrassment, and perhaps even humiliation, because I think the arguments of the opposition are valid when he considers the elements that contributed perhaps to his election and to the election of others in Alberta in 1957 and 1958. I say that because there has been delay and confusion in the policy of this government with respect to the development of this very important Canadian National Railways system for national development.

I do not need to refer to the campaign speeches the Prime Minister of this country (Mr. Diefenbaker) made in 1957. It was clear then that he was not expecting any help from others in the development of the north. He said, "We will build a railway". As it turns out, after their stomping around the country, four and a half years later, as hon. members on the government side have reminded us, we are only now getting some suggestion through a legislative bill that authority is available for going forward with this railway. If we have any doubt about the forthrightness of this government, irrespective of election campaigns-

subsubtopic: CONSTRUCTION OF LINE TO GREAT SLAVE LAKE
speechtext: You have no idea.

subsubtopic: CONSTRUCTION OF LINE TO GREAT SLAVE LAKE
speechtext:
-let us look at their sincerity in speaking to parliament. I refer to the speech from the throne of May 12, 1958. This government talked about a royal commission. They were passing the buck. This government, enthused with the vote it had received from the Canadian electorate, said:
In order to promote our national development on the frontier in the north you will be asked-
That is, we in parliament would be asked:
-to authorize the construction of a railway to Great Slave lake. My ministers regard this as a major step in the establishment of productive industry on an economic basis in the Northwest Territories.
What was the economic climate at the time of the speech from the throne on May 12, 1958? It was the lowest it had been since the end of the second world war, though we have had it lower since under the Conservative regime. What has happened? After that great statement, after the endorsation which they received, we got, on December 20, another refresher, Oh, there were palliatives and aspirins given with respect to this in the meantime. On December 20, 1960, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) felt that he would emulate the great record of the late minister of trade and commerce, the Right Hon. Mr. Howe by putting forward certain proposals for economic advancement at the right time. And he said as reported on page 1023 of Hansard:
We are also proposing to commence a number of specific major projects which will lay the groundwork for the resumption and acceleration of the long-term growth of our natural resource industries.
That was on December 20. That was after the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) had said in 1960 that we were just about to give this fillip to the economy. This was after the speech from the throne of 1958, part of which I have recited; and I have no hesitation in
Canadian National Railways saying that this is a government of talkers, not of doers in the economic field. They are expert chiefly at procrastination and indecision with respect to economic matters.
In so far as this bill is concerned I should like to ask a question or two. What was there from the beginning to have prevented this government from asking the Canadian Pacific Railway which, I think, has ultimate ownership of the primary mining entity in the area, to build this line? To what extent did the government pursue that line of investigation? In the second place, I would ask: is this, as so many speakers up to now have described it, a subsidy, or is it a capital investment made on behalf of the people of Canada with the idea that it will be good for Canada and likely to pay off? My third question is: if this is a subsidy in the opinion of the government, why should the government not implement a policy of taking, in partnership with those others who contribute to the advancement of the economy, equity stock in the Pine Point railway? Everybody else who invests in such things aspires ultimately to some share of the capital stock. I should also like to know whether or not this so-called investment by the railroad-or is it the government?-includes concessions for freight rates which will ultimately be assessed against the railroad. I have experience of a natural resource development in my riding, a development of extreme importance, and I refer to Steep Rock Iron Mines. While the company did not, as I understand it, contribute directly to the capital investment involving improvements to the railway line, as a result of the traffic to be produced there was ultimately a moral obligation on the C.N.R. with respect to the rate per ton which would be charged by the government-owned railroad on the iron ore transported to the lakehead for distribution. I understand that arbitrarily the C.N.R. has increased that rate by 25 per cent. Is there anything of that kind involved here? I think the minister should give us some assurance as to the relationship between guaranteed tonnages, if any, and the capital investment which either the government or the C.N.R. are prepared to make with respect to this railway. I think it was significant for the minister to have said that in certain circumstances certain variations might occur in the future.
According to information I have received I believe there is a possible ore tonnage of 120 million tons involved in this development. I do not think the minister said anything to indicate what the economists of either the government or the C.N.R. consider to be a firm estimate. I am well aware that promoters of mining enterprises sometimes get a little excited, a little enthused as to the prospects

Canadian National Railways of the property in which they are interested, and conscientiously enlarge their estimates of what they think the nearby or ultimate production will be. I have heard estimates that the ultimate production of this resource may be as much as $2J billion. This amounts to between 17 and 20 per cent of our present national debt, so we are talking about something which is of very great importance.
But I come back to the question of timing, judgment and leadership. I say to the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) who is not now in his place-

subsubtopic: CONSTRUCTION OF LINE TO GREAT SLAVE LAKE
speechtext: He is over there.

subsubtopic: CONSTRUCTION OF LINE TO GREAT SLAVE LAKE
speechtext:
I see him. I say to him
that he cannot repeat himself too often. He cannot say to his electors that this is imminent and to be done at once when we hear tonight-and I questioned the minister about it-that completion of this enterprise which has been talked about so much on political platforms cannot be expected until 1966. I said "Oh," and the minister confirmed that it would not be completed until 1966. The hon. member for Peace River was interviewed by the Edmonton Journal on December 5, 1960. Of course, he forgot about the delay which had taken place. That statement in the speech from the throne did not suggest for a moment that any royal commission would be intervening. However, he said that we could expect completion of the railway within two years. That was in December, 1960. It is now almost December of the year 1961. While it was not mentioned by the Minister of Transport, before we proceed to pass this bill we and the people in the area concerned must have a more detailed estimate of progress not only in connection with the survey which parliament has already approved but with respect to final completion. The government has information from the company on its files as to its intentions with respect to completion of the mill and its readiness to have available traffic for the railway and the government which apparently, under this bill, is guaranteeing certain losses. That information must be given in committee before the bill is finally passed. This is of great consequence to the people who reside in this area.
The Minister of Transport, as a member of the government, is very respectful of northern mining. In my dealings with the mining fraternity I have found them to be generally very fair, extremely knowledgeable and-if you will permit me Mr. Speaker, -very conservative in their approval of activity in this parliament not only under the former but under the present administration.

With respect to the Pine Point railway may I quote from an editorial which appeared in The Northern Miner of April 27, 1961:
Consistency of word and deed is also imperative. We have a government which encourages the people at large to think that there is something shameful about foreigners, like Americans, developing our natural resources, and which has given mild verbal urgings to Canadians to do the developing themselves. Yet when an opportunity to have a big mining project like Pine Point developed 100 per cent with Canadian talent, money, and ownership, where is the government? Is it mired to the knees in the muskeg of indecision?
Another point: the country could very well do with the extra employment that development of this new mine would provide. Why, then, wait any longer?
This article appeared in April, 1961 after this same publication had pointed out that in 1958, in the speech from the throne the government indicated there was to be no royal commission, no equivocation, that it was going forward just as had been suggested in the election campaigns of 1957 and 1958. Even this evening we are denied answers to the question "How soon will this railway be complete?" except that we might take the answer of the minister, 1966, after another election.
But what about the survey? Parliament has previously taken an attitude with respect to survey expenditures. How far toward completion is the survey? The hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) said that the idea of delay and confusion existed solely in the mind of the hon. member for Laurier who made an excellent speech. I am sure the people of northern Alberta will not welcome that kind of criticism from the hon. member for Edmonton West in reply to a speech made by the hon. member for Laurier who indicated the desire of this party to get on with this project which means so much to Canada as a whole and is equivalent to some of the projects that were undertaken on timely occasions by the previous government, to which projects I have already referred and which were undertaken at a time when unemployment required that kind of stimulus.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. If It is possible for a humble backbencher to be misquoted, may I say that the quotation attributed to me to the effect that I said this railway would be built and completed within two years from December of 1960, is not a correct statement and is one I did not make.

subsubtopic: CONSTRUCTION OF LINE TO GREAT SLAVE LAKE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I accept the hon. member's correction but I think both you and he will know that I have in my hand a photostatic copy of the Edmonton Journal of that date.

subsubtopic: CONSTRUCTION OF LINE TO GREAT SLAVE LAKE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words with respect to the railroad leading to the north country. I did not blow in at the tail end of the storm as did my friend the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River who just addressed us. I know something about the north. I have lived there for over 40 years.

subsubtopic: CONSTRUCTION OF LINE TO GREAT SLAVE LAKE
speechtext: We refer to Kenora as northern Ontario.

subsubtopic: CONSTRUCTION OF LINE TO GREAT SLAVE LAKE
speechtext:
Just recently I flew over that part of the country where the proposed railway will be built. This is a part of a country that contains the world's largest deposits of that kind of mineral. These vast reserves await development. The proposed railway will serve the 8,000 people who now live in the area. If the refinery is constructed there will be a city there with a population of between 25,000 to 30,000. We need that type of development in the north.
The part of the country to which I am referring is not like this part of the country. That area is filled with opportunities for people to make fortunes. The same opportunity awaits the railway. It will be of real value. I am surprised that people like the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River should knock and buck a project of this nature which could lead to prosperity that would benefit the whole economy.
The north country is the richest land there is in Canada; there can be no argument about that. The area I referred to is adjacent to the Peace River country. In the Peace River country there exists the richest farmland in Canada. In the southern part there are 8,000 acres of arable land awaiting development by farmers who are not afraid to work.
I believe that the Pine Point railway is the key to the development of this area. The people there are waiting for it and I believe they will see it come into existence. It has taken this government, a government with a vision, to implement this project. The former government was too scared, and it just dreamed. This is a government that gets out and does what is necessary.
